SYMNAV · MAIN → #149 · ONE ARCHITECTURE DELTA
Who owns
what survives?

Daemon machinery leaves the CLI. Reusable workspace retention leaves TypeScript. The new boundaries separate a process, an accepted request, a delivery, and a semantic turn.

26 PRs · 254 changed files
+27,533 / −8,698 lines in the supplied delta.

117 authored decisions + 24 additional recovered choices. 44 policy records. Five deliberately absent deadlines.

b6801eb → d070023
＋

Keep the workshop. Clear its scratch paper at the right boundary.

Lossy analogy: tools = retained workspace objects; scratch paper = semantic memoization. Release clears caches without closing the session or cancelling existing callers.

Package inventory; arrows above show selected interactions.
A package boundary is not a process boundary. The daemon package has no internal package imports; its worker loads a host-supplied executor module that uses core and TypeScript.
The seams to carry
with the picture

The spec asks for unchanged behavior. The visible decision surface also includes an awaited release change, protocol generation 5, relative control-path normalization, removed CLI test scenarios, relaxed test budgets, and a PR-template edit.

02 / hold the shape
Six ownership questions

The map’s six entrances. The decision sheet below is the complete top layer of recovered choices.

01 · 5 PRS
Remember the workspace
CLI scopes + TypeScript retention
↓ Core session, transactions, project graph, turn scope

Keep workspace objects between requests; publish candidates at explicit boundaries; expire semantic memoization after successful refresh or at release. TypeScript keeps syntax and semantic algorithms.

#123 · #124 · #126 · #127 · #128 ↗
02 · 3 PRS
Give policy one owner
Telemetry path lookup + scattered CLI numbers
↓ CLI resolves environment; daemon owns a frozen policy

One canonical path and one complete policy snapshot cross process and worker boundaries. Consumers require slices. Public DaemonClient may default its optional policy. Numeric defaults and five absent deadlines remain explicit below.

#129 · #130 · #131 ↗
03 · 5 PRS
Name the crossing
CLI types, argv inference, embedded formatting
↓ Daemon contracts + injected host + renderer

CLI supplies command identity and the executor module. Daemon owns failure and admission vocabularies, ordered guards, validation and byte sequencing. Renderer owns lifecycle bytes. Protocol generation advances from 4 to 5.

#132 · #133 · #134 · #135 · #136 ↗
04 · 7 PRS
Separate a socket from a transfer
LocalDaemonTransport
↓ Codec, validator, receiver, capture, clients, server

A connection ends at disconnect; durable transfer state survives a fetch. Reattachment starts fresh capture for the same accepted request. Recovery budgets are independent; exhausted accepted work is not replayed locally.

#137 · #138 · #139 · #140 · #141 · #142 · #143 ↗
05 · 4 PRS
Separate a turn from its delivery
WorkspaceDaemon
↓ Activity projector, generation manager, delivery and execution sessions

One FIFO executes newly accepted work; the ledger keeps original identity, delivery tracks the latest attachment, and a worker manager fences generations. Warm-up sampling gates readiness. Acceptance-based idle timing and sampled status are preserved.

#144 · #145 · #146 · #147 ↗
06 · 2 PRS
Close the package boundary
CLI reaches daemon mechanisms
↓ CLI → DaemonClient; package owns mechanisms

#148 stages package copies while the CLI still uses its compatibility graph; #149 switches consumers and removes it. The final public surface has no Node ambient requirement, policy serialization is internal, and tests get a read-only inspector.

#148 · #149 ↗

The decision sheet

Every row is an entrance. Reasons and evidence are attached to the same decision ID.

Stated means a reason is in a PR, commit or inspected plan. Unexplained means no reason was found there. Neither is a correctness verdict. Early PR choices are marked in their historical order; #149’s final API closures are visible under “Close the package boundary.”

The core project graph traverses configuration references FIFO, preserves configured-owner order, uses the first owner for primary lookup and sends unowned files to an inferred project.

x-graph-order · #126 · reason & evidence ↗
Release projects sequentially; backends concurrently
unexplained

A project graph awaits each configured project in order, then its inferred project; a rejection stops that sequence. A workspace session uses Promise.all across backends and remains reusable.

x-release-order · #126 · reason & evidence ↗
Atomicity is local to one publication
stated

Backend refresh publishes one candidate; ensureFiles retains earlier per-file progress. A later failing backend prevents a WorkspaceSession scope from returning but does not undo an earlier backend commit.

x-transaction-scope · #128 · reason & evidence ↗
Keep three newly recorded behavior changes deferred
stated

Selection refresh still evicts omitted source bytes. Idle timing still starts at construction and resets at acceptance. Sibling-byte retention, readiness-armed idle time and completion-based idle time are documented follow-ups, not shipped behavior.

x-deferred · #123 · reason & evidence ↗
Expose generic core bases and make prepared-file access asynchronous
stated

Core gains revisioned preparation/state and project-graph contracts. TypeScriptWorkspaceState extends the new base; fileEntries now returns a promise. PreparedFileIndex, PreparedFileRevision and TypeScriptFileRevision disappear from the TypeScript package root.

x-backend-api · #124 · reason & evidence ↗
Return exact values; retain async failure; retry sync throws
stated

Each handle stores the factory result unchanged. Rejected promises stay cached for the turn; a synchronous throw inserts nothing and the next access retries. Old promise settlement cannot replace a new-turn entry.

p-identity · #127 · reason & evidence ↗
Cache positions, rehydrate nodes on each lookup
stated

The sixth cache uses relative-path:source-offset keys and stores location arrays, including empty arrays. Returned node arrays are rebuilt per access. Identity caches use formatted symbol identities; callers and refs share reference discovery.

p-position · #127 · reason & evidence ↗
The backend now observes project-cleanup completion and failure
unexplained

Both versions clear caches before project cleanup settles. Base backend release fulfills while cleanup is pending; head backend release stays pending and propagates rejection. This is an observable async boundary change within a preservation-framed PR.

p-release · #127 · reason & evidence ↗
Narrow beginTurn from a snapshot to its file array
unexplained

TypeScriptSemanticQueryService.beginTurn now takes readonly WorkspaceFile[]; the backend passes snapshot.files. The service continues to hold those files after release.

p-files · #127 · reason & evidence ↗
Clear entries; keep reusable handles and existing callers
unexplained

beginTurn and release both clear every registered map synchronously. Handles remain registered; there is no disposal or eviction API. Clearing does not cancel pending work or revoke objects already returned, and a later lookup may refill the cache during release.

p-handles · #127 · reason & evidence ↗
Add ten characterization/lifecycle tests; keep prior assertions
stated

#127 adds six semantic-service cases and four core-scope cases. Existing semantic assertions remain; one existing release call gains await. This experiment ran both affected suites: 15 tests passed.

Policy snapshots travel whole; internal process/worker serialization is not a public host API at #149. The facade can derive system policy; production consumers receive required policy slices. These are code policies, with no user flag or configuration knob for thresholds.

06 / inspect the grounding
What this page actually observed

Code and source history ground the map. This experiment does not certify the stack.

Read all 26 PR bodies and commit messages, both supplied deltas programmatically, the architecture/policy/follow-up plans, and selected final and intermediate source and test files. The precomputed overview files contain path headings but no useful symbol output. #127’s two focused suites passed 15 tests; the stack’s claimed suite totals remain author reports. No full-stack behavioral parity run was performed here.

01
Make the caller supply the limits
Local defaults + per-consumer knobs
→
Required policy inputs
Output capture, spooling, framing, resources, lifecycle and diagnostics read the existing snapshot. The operational implementations stay in apps/cli.
Reason: Omitted composition must not recreate local defaults.
stated

02
Keep the operating envelope
Existing values, formulas and untimed waits
→
Same values, one policy definition
Defaults are retained. Memory limits still depend on host memory. No user tuning is added. Healthy startup, accepted completion and worker output acknowledgement still have no deadline; startup silence and result eviction remain deferred.
Reason: The architecture spec requires behavior preservation, one policy owner and no user tuning.
stated

03
Let composition choose the response clock
Status action supplies 100 ms directly
→
Status-observer purpose selects 100 ms
The purpose belongs to a transport instance, not to a message kind. Ordinary lifecycle and execution-status exchanges keep 250 ms; execute admission keeps its separate 5 s clock.
Reason: Status observation and ordinary execution-status requests have distinct deadlines.
stated

04
Count attempts in their own scopes
One-shot reattach / resume / startup retry
→
Three numeric limits, all default to 1
Reattachment spans accepted execution; fetch-resume state belongs to each execute attempt, as it already did in base. Startup retry is separate and counts child exit or lost warm-up.
Reason: Each reattached execute attempt needs its own fetch-resume allowance; startup retains a fresh launch after failure.
stated

05
Expose the reattached completion's error
Recovery failure rethrows first accepted-close error
→
Later completion can expose its own error
After an accepted close, a corrupt completion on the reattachment reaches the caller as corrupt instead of closed. Failure to obtain the reattached receipt still preserves the preceding error.
unexplained

Defaults hidden in consumers and helpers

Snapshot → sections → fields → numbers
Some consumers take several sections, others one field or a bare number. The worker parent reparses the snapshot for a chunk limit; stored output keeps an optional internal cap. Transport keeps writeChunkSize and outputDirectory options.

Tests tune production constructors

Seven helper files translate into policies
Test-only wrappers preserve legacy calls and construct validated snapshots. Existing validation now governs their overrides: ordered output and memory limits, integers and positive polling intervals.
Reason: Tests need small limits without restoring production tuning seams.

Simplified picture: related modules are grouped and incidental imports are omitted. Source ownership is separate from process topology; this is not a runtime trace.

The complete overview is the picture plus all 24 choices below.
Each choice opens the same fact at greater detail, then exact source. Stated means a reason was found; unexplained means the sources did not explain that choice. Neither is a verdict.
WHAT THIS CHANGE ASKS THE HUMAN TO UNDERSTAND
The decisions, including the small ones.
Read them in order →
01
Two implementations coexist

The package owns the new composition. The CLI continues through its existing graph.

CHOICE 01
STATED
↗
Stage the package; leave the CLI connected to its copies

The new client and mechanisms exist alongside 38 frozen CLI production files. This PR does not switch the shipped CLI to DaemonClient.

PR body: ownership relocation and host invocation coordination need separate review boundaries.

CHOICE 02
STATED
↗
Freeze paths and source bytes, normalizing CRLF

A fixed SHA-256 digest and a count of 38 protect the compatibility set. CRLF becomes LF; other source changes still change the digest.

Commit “Specify portable daemon compatibility hashing” records portability; the test explicitly exercises CRLF and a changed source.

CHOICE 03
STATED
↗
Give private mechanisms ten directory owners

Ten owner directories place mechanisms in a daemon package with no other internal production dependency. The completion spool gets a package-local record codec instead of importing the CLI output utility.

Architecture spec: give daemon policy and mechanism one home; daemon must not depend on navigation or CLI implementation.

CHOICE 04
STATED
↗
Make process and worker entries executable package subpaths

The manifest exposes process-entry and worker-entry as side-effect-only entries. Launcher and worker resolve those files relative to package modules.

Architecture spec names real process and worker entries as part of daemon package extraction; commits explicitly require exhaustive entry exports.

02
A host hands over execution

Syntax and product knowledge stay with the host; daemon decisions sit behind a client.

CHOICE 05
STATED
↗
Pass product knowledge in; return bytes and reports

The host supplies state path, version, enabled flag, executor factory, executor module URL, readiness probe and optional policy. Each execute call supplies workspace, command, argv, cwd and telemetry flag.

Architecture spec: the daemon moves bytes for an injected executor and must not know navigation internals or parse CLI syntax.

CHOICE 06
STATED
↗
Keep Node out of public declarations

The public façade describes a small runtime port and dynamically imports the Node-backed implementation. The façade’s declarations do not pull Node ambient types into hosts.

PR body: host declarations must not acquire Node ambient dependencies.

CHOICE 07
UNEXPLAINED
↗
Begin loading at construction; retain one runtime promise

Constructing DaemonClient starts the dynamic load immediately. Execute and control await the same promise; a rejected load is not retried by these methods.

The declaration-isolation reason is stated. No separate reason was found for starting in the constructor or retaining a rejected promise.

CHOICE 08
STATED
↗
Reuse lifecycle composition and keep action-specific results

Start/status/stop have precise overloads. Status gets a separate response timeout; disabled blocks start and sends execute locally, while status and stop still run. Control errors propagate.

The architecture specifies lifecycle reports; the policy distinguishes status response timing. The client’s lifecycle tests state the disabled and failure behavior.

CHOICE 09
STATED
↗
Let the host name the readiness execution

The client passes a host-supplied command and argv to startup. Readiness still executes with cold mode and telemetry off; the internal coordinator retains a --version default.

The architecture keeps CLI syntax with the host; commits explicitly specify a host-owned readiness probe. Control-plane-only readiness remains a deferred behavior.

03
A decision ends the search

Short-circuit routing and retry authority determine which side effects happen.

CHOICE 10
STATED
↗
Stop after the first routing decision

Record present → not starting → version compatible → responsive. Read once and observe at most once. A starting record wins even when its version is old.

PR body: the first routing decision must prevent every later side effect. Architecture spec makes the order explicit and independently testable.

CHOICE 11
STATED
↗
Run cold work now; trigger only selected warm-ups

Disabled, starting and recovery execute cold. Absence executes cold plus an independent trigger; dead/incompatible execute fallback plus a trigger. Every local attempt gets a fresh executor with no resource sampler.

The architecture preserves routing and local execution behavior. Existing CLI routing and new client characterization both express independent warm-up.

CHOICE 12
STATED
↗
Let retry-safety authorize local re-execution

Only a DaemonTransportError marked retrySafe permits local fallback. Submitted uncertainty, accepted failures and malformed warm completions return controlled warm failures; they do not replay.

PR body: replay safety belongs to the daemon client. The architecture keeps one owner for the retry-safety decision.

CHOICE 13
STATED
↗
Own result capture, controlled output and cleanup inside the package

The client creates capture from output policy, spilling to the OS temporary directory, and constructs failure output itself. A private capture factory port stays internal; callers consume and dispose the returned output.

PR body: warm transfer cleanup and replay safety belong to the client, rather than host-provided storage or output factories.

CHOICE 14
STATED
↗
Dispose a malformed warm result before replacing it

A non-integer exit code or missing output becomes an incomplete-request result. The package client attempts disposal of available malformed output; the CLI dispatcher’s older check does not.

PR body assigns warm transfer cleanup to the client; the new test explicitly requires disposal before returning the controlled result.

04
Ownership becomes explicit

Clock, startup credentials, coordinates and request authentication keep their own boundaries.

CHOICE 15
STATED
↗
Use the daemon’s wall and monotonic clock everywhere it was threaded

Wall time drives lifetime, registry leases, controller waits, ledger timestamps and replacement windows. Monotonic time drives queue/worker durations; the queue’s standalone default changes to monotonic.

Architecture spec assigns wall and monotonic clock ownership to the daemon; PR retains existing lifetime behavior.

CHOICE 16
STATED
↗
Keep construction/acceptance-based idle timing; defer two changes

The deadline starts at construction and resets on navigation acceptance. Completion only checks it; readiness does not reset it. Readiness-armed and completion-based timing are added to the follow-up spec.

PR body: changing lifetime behavior is explicitly deferred rather than folded into extraction.

CHOICE 17
STATED
↗
Make registry ownership matching canonical, with narrow and exact expectations

Callers delegate startup equality and cleanup to the registry. Every match checks identity and instance; supplied token, kind, PID, timestamps and revision narrow the match. Full observed owners are compared exactly.

Architecture spec requires one owner for lock-ownership checks; commits separately specify canonical authority and narrow coordinates.

CHOICE 18
UNEXPLAINED
↗
Let the process coordinator adopt and validate launch coordinates

WorkspaceDaemon becomes DaemonProcessCoordinator. It receives the complete coordinate object and required clock, validates identity/endpoint, and uses that endpoint for listening. Callback wiring keeps execution, delivery, worker and resource owners separate.

The spec names the process-coordinator split. No explicit reason was found for moving coordinate validation from entry to constructor or the detailed construction API choices.

CHOICE 19
UNEXPLAINED
↗
Characterize the existing authentication order and its exceptions

Identify/terminate/kill check instance+token. Other messages first check protocol+instance; execute and result operations add token checks. Ping and stop keep only protocol+instance authentication.

New tests explicitly preserve these different envelopes. No reason for the asymmetry or the order was found in the supplied rationale sources.

05
The evidence changes owners too

Moving a test and preserving everything it observed are separate choices.

CHOICE 20
STATED
↗
Move 37 mechanism test files and give them generic fixtures

Mechanism tests move from CLI to package. Generic executors, canonical-path/output helpers and duplicated policy helpers remove CLI implementation imports. tsx is added as a daemon development dependency.

Architecture spec: tests importing mechanisms move into the package or use its public surface; commit “Keep executor fixture package-independent” states the fixture boundary.

CHOICE 21
UNEXPLAINED
↗
Narrow worker tests’ observation of the real CLI executor

The integrated CLI version-mismatch case disappears; a direct CLI factory rejection test is added. The readiness case uses a generic executor and removes startup/result timing expectations.

Package-independent fixtures have a stated reason. No reason was found for losing these specific timing assertions or changing mismatch coverage from worker classification to factory rejection.

CHOICE 22
UNEXPLAINED
↗
Delete CLI entry tests; add built package entry evidence

Two app entry tests are removed. New package boundary, export and built-process/worker tests exercise package ownership, startup configuration and failure cleanup. Windows and other-platform cleanup expectations differ.

Real package entries are explicitly requested. No equivalence argument was found for removing the app-entry assertions; the Windows branch is specified by a commit, without explanatory body.

CHOICE 23
UNEXPLAINED
↗
Retire policy-testing and redraw source guard coverage

The policy-testing export and its lint restriction/tests disappear; helpers move into both test trees. Exact root/entry export checks remain. A new raw-clock scan examines only lifecycle siblings, not all daemon directories.

The old export was labeled temporary, but no explicit removal rationale or reason for the local scope of the new clock scan was found.

CHOICE 24
UNEXPLAINED
↗
Run daemon package test files serially

A new Vitest configuration sets fileParallelism to false. This changes how this package’s test files are scheduled.

Not named in the PR’s stated intent. No scheduling reason was found in the PR body, commit messages or inspected specifications.

1	Backend release waits for project release and carries its failure	unexplained	behavior outside spec ask	Restores main's result for today's sync projects. Spec: no behavior change while restructuring; not in follow-ups spec.
2	Failure asymmetry becomes core's generic contract	stated as preservation	kept	Rejected or empty promise stays for the turn; a synchronous throw stores nothing and re-runs; an old turn's promise never refills a new turn.

(workspace-daemon.ts:1041–1053, monitor.ts:194–196)
Figure 4.9 Different diagnostic trail per build. read from code at #127 (no daemon file differs on #126); the full daemon was not run
CONTEXT FOR DECISIONS 1 AND 5
Spec plans/005/daemon-architecture-functional-spec.md:17–28: "Behavior is unchanged … failure path behaves as it does today"; "no 'it was obviously a bug' override. Behavior defects found during restructuring are recorded in daemon-follow-ups-functional-spec.md". That file has no entry on transient release (checked at #127 and at #149).
#126 made ProjectGraph.releaseTransientResources async (commit d01ab95 "Release project resources sequentially"); the service's un-awaited call dates from #117 (97e2cfb). #126's body says it keeps "refresh or semantic lookup behavior"; release is not mentioned.
The pending window of decision 5 needs an async project release. TypeScript projects release synchronously (typescript-project-graph.ts:78). The core interface allows async (ProjectWithTransientResources: void | Promise<void>, project-graph.ts:64), and the spec expects future hosts (:7–11).
4.9 Decisions in depth
JUDGE · SAME 12 AS 4.0

Each card: what was chosen, the reason if one exists (verbatim), what is new versus kept, and the facts that bear on it. No card says whether a choice is right.

1 · Backend release waits for project release and carries its failure unexplained behavior
CHOSEN
await this.semanticQueries.releaseTransientResources() (backend:88) and await this.projects?.releaseTransientResources() (service:131).
REASON
None found. The PR body shows it (After diagram: "awaited release boundary"; public surface: releaseTransientResources(): Promise<void>) and commit 5 is titled "Specify awaited semantic resource release", with no body.
VS BUILDS
Real: main rejects · #126 resolves, unhandled rejection, worker dies · #127 rejects. With async project release: main and #126 resolve before it settles; #127 waits. Table 4.1
ASKED FOR?
Spec asks core to own the turn-scoped cache lifecycle and keeps every failure path unchanged; behavior fixes go to the follow-ups spec, which has no entry for this.
WEIGH
For today's synchronous TS projects this restores main. For async projects it is a new contract. Both readings are supported by the runs.
2 · Failure asymmetry becomes core's generic contract stated as preservation
CHOSEN
getOrCreate stores whatever the factory returns, including a Promise that later rejects or an empty result; a synchronous throw stores nothing; clearing never waits for or listens to old Promises.
REASON
"this layer moves only cache lifetime out of TypeScript while preserving all six algorithms, key spaces, promise/value identities, and failure behavior."
KEPT?
Yes. Steps 5–6 match on all builds; the 5 characterization tests pass on #126 code (10/10).
WEIGH
Every future TurnScopedCacheScope consumer inherits sticky rejections for a whole turn. The PR does not discuss other consumers; at #149 there are none.
3 · One scope with six handles, not one shared map stated
CHOSEN
createCache<Key, Value>() called six times on one scope (service:32–55).
REASON
"Chose one scope with six handles over one shared map, because the existing queries have independent key and value spaces."
FACTS
Five handles hold the identical key src/lib.ts::target with five value types (4.5, real dump). The PR names the shared map as the alternative; no other alternative is discussed.
4 · Scope exported from @symnav/core stated by spec
CHOSEN
export { TurnScopedCacheScope, type TurnScopedCache } (core index.ts:152).
REASON
Spec: "Shared in core: … turn-scoped query cache lifecycle." (plans/005/daemon-architecture-functional-spec.md:58–60)
FACTS
No new package dependency: the service already imported @symnav/core. Consumers: 1 (TS semantic query service) at #127; still 1 at #149, where scope and service files are byte-identical to #127.
5 · Empty caches synchronously, before awaiting project release stated
CHOSEN
service:130 this.cacheScope.releaseTransientResources() then :131 await this.projects?.releaseTransientResources().
REASON
"Chose synchronous cache clearing before project release over clearing after the await, because released semantics must be unavailable while release is pending or rejecting."
KEPT?
Order kept: #126 and main also cleared first (base service:126–127). The await is decision 1.
WEIGH
The pending window exists only with async project release. TS projects release synchronously; the daemon worker, the only production caller, runs release and commands one at a time. The PR's test opens the window with a fake async graph. The core interface and the spec's future hosts allow async.
6 · Next turn begins only after refresh succeeds stated
CHOSEN
beginTurn stays the last statement before return in refresh (backend:83).
REASON
"Chose to begin the next turn only after refresh succeeds over clearing at refresh entry, because failed refresh must preserve the current successful turn."
KEPT?
Same position on main and #126. New test "preserves the current turn when backend refresh fails" passes on #126 code. Real: steps 10–11.
7 · Map.has before Map.get, not truthiness stated
CHOSEN
if (this.values.has(key)) return this.values.get(key) as Value; (scope:15).
REASON
"Chose Map.has before Map.get over truthiness checks, because undefined is a valid cached value."
FACTS
All six TS handles store Promises or arrays; none can be falsy, so the old truthiness checks behaved identically. Core test "returns each exact factory value once per key and handle" caches undefined.
8 · beginTurn(files) replaces beginTurn(snapshot) unexplained
CHOSEN
beginTurn(files: readonly WorkspaceFile[]) on the exported TypeScriptSemanticQueryService (service:63).
REASON
None found; listed under "Public surface" without a reason.
FACTS
Old body used only snapshot.files (base service:50). Only caller: TypeScriptBackend.refresh. The final commit edits four test call sites to match.
9 · Scope created inside the service, not injected unexplained
CHOSEN
private readonly cacheScope = new TurnScopedCacheScope(); (service:31).
REASON
None found. PR diagram: "Service owns Scope".
FACTS
Backend, router and daemon reach the caches only through the service's beginTurn and releaseTransientResources. Other shape (this chapter's example, not discussed in the PR): the backend creates the scope and passes it in.
10 · Handles expose only getOrCreate unexplained
CHOSEN
Exported interface TurnScopedCache has one method (scope:1–3). clear() lives on the internal TurnScopedCacheHandle.
REASON
None found.
FACTS
No way to invalidate one handle or one key. Invalidation is all six at once.
11 · Scope's beginTurn() and releaseTransientResources() share one body unexplained
CHOSEN
Both call this.clear() (scope:35–41).
REASON
None found.
FACTS
Core test "clears every handle at turn and release boundaries" pins both names, including a double release.
12 · File lives in core/src/backend/ unexplained
CHOSEN
packages/core/src/backend/turn-scoped-cache-scope.ts.
REASON
None found.
FACTS
Neighbors: backend-router.ts, language-backend.ts, revisioned-backend-state.ts, errors.ts.

text:
Skip to decisions
SYMNAV / PR 131
05 · STATIC STRUCTURE × RUNTIME TOPOLOGY
Where policy
becomes behavior.

The snapshot already traveled to the daemon and its worker. This change connects the mechanisms to its values: limits, clocks, and retry allowances.

BEFORE
Policy snapshot
→ already delivered →
Mechanisms
← configured by ←
Local defaults + knobs
AFTER
Policy snapshot
→ required inputs →
Mechanisms
Same package locations. Same processes.

Simplified intuition: the real inputs are sections and, at leaf calls, individual values. The two maps below show the boundaries separately.

What stays in place
@symnav/daemon owns the policy; the mechanisms still live in apps/cli. The CLI process talks to a separate daemon process containing a worker thread. Policy defaults and serialization are unchanged in #131. Users get no new tuning flags.

60
changed files
+1,298 / −544
Whole change
Static map ↗
Runtime map ↗
Mechanisms & evidence
01 / THE WHOLE CHANGE
Twelve decisions to carry into the maps.

Stated = a reason exists in the supplied PR or policy record.
Unexplained = no reason found in the inspected inputs.

01
STATED
Make composition mandatory

Consumers require policy sections instead of optional operational numbers and local defaults. Code stays in the CLI package; the policy package and its defaults already exist. This is an input contract, not proof of value provenance.

Open mechanism & source ↗
02
STATED
Use one set of byte capacities

Capture, spool, file decoding, worker validation and socket framing receive policy-backed caps. Chunk, inline, per-result and aggregate limits retain distinct jobs; the default values stay the same.

Open mechanism & source ↗
03
STATED
Read the derived memory limits

The app’s duplicate memory-policy class and reconstruction disappear. RSS thresholds, worker heap limit, sampling cadence and replacement circuit use the supplied resources section; ready/status records report its hard cap.

Open mechanism & source ↗
04
STATED
Keep distinct clocks and retention limits

Startup, shutdown, idle life, acknowledgement waiting, log rotation/queueing and trace retention take their own policy fields. Equal-looking intervals remain separate. Healthy startup and accepted completion still have no total deadline.

Open mechanism & source ↗
05
STATED
Choose the timeout by caller purpose

Socket inactivity timers use 100 ms for status observation and 250 ms for ordinary lifecycle / execution-status. Execute admission uses 5 s, disabled after acceptance. A request named “status” does not automatically get the observer timeout.

Open mechanism & source ↗
06
STATED
Put numbers on existing retry scopes

Startup child retries and accepted-execute reattachments become numeric loops. Fetch resume has a per-execute counter. Defaults are one each. The two delivery scopes already existed in base; reattachment keeps the same request identity.

Open mechanism & source ↗
07
UNEXPLAINED
Let a later completion failure escape

The reattachment rewrite changes error selection: a later completion rejection can replace the original accepted-close error. A failure to obtain the reattached receipt still rethrows the prior error. No separate rationale was found.

Open mechanism & source ↗
08
UNEXPLAINED
Leave fetch failure as a terminal path

The numeric resume check sits on the original execute socket. A failed result-fetch still goes to fail; increasing the field does not introduce a retry loop inside fetchCompletion. No reason for that boundary was found.

Open mechanism & source ↗
09
STATED
Move compatibility knobs into tests

Seven new test helpers translate legacy options into policies; a logger adapter is local to its test. Existing tests and benchmarks switch imports. Production constructors lose numeric tuning options while the validated test factory remains the override route.

Open mechanism & source ↗
10
UNEXPLAINED
Change test inputs and recorded data

Tiny-limit normalization removes spilled-file evidence from some single-chunk cleanup tests. Helpers create output directories, accept an unused legacy memory-cap option, and expand benchmark resource records. Spill fixtures change chunk sizes and thresholds. These specific choices are unexplained.

Open mechanism & source ↗
11
UNEXPLAINED
Retire the local derivation suite and unused knob

The app’s memory derivation suite, including its literal 250 ms assertion, is deleted; related package tests already exist. Startup tests lose an unused timeout option. Policy-consumption, tiny-chunk, timeout-purpose and retry tests are added.

Open mechanism & source ↗
12
UNEXPLAINED
Enforce retired names with a source scan

The meta-test expands a production-source blacklist of retired constants, option names and the duplicate policy class. This checks source spellings rather than following values through the system. The enforcement technique is unexplained.

Open mechanism & source ↗

Scope of the promise: required TypeScript inputs do not prove where a value came from. Leaf codecs still receive numbers; the registry still permits an explicit grace argument; transport still accepts a write-fragment size. These existing seams remain visible below.

K8STATED + UNEXPLAINEDBuild every mechanism once per client, not per request
Constructor builds 1 registry, 2 transports (250 ms / 100 ms lifecycle timeout), 1 terminator, 1 launcher, 1 startup coordinator, 2 controllers, 4 record observers (3 built inside coordinator and controllers). K5STATEDSeparate public declarations from the Node runtime
DaemonClient (64 lines) imports only types. Its constructor starts import(runtimeModuleUrl) through a string variable; execute/control await the same promise. The facade’s type-dependency closure has 7 source files. The runtime still uses Node. Root API grows by 1 class + 4 types.

K7STATEDRoute with 4 ordered, lazy guards
record present → not starting → version match → responsive. First answer wins; registry read and observation memoized per decision. Absent and fallback routes trigger background startup without waiting; starting/recovering stay local without a trigger. The 12-scenario table matches the dispatcher’s route outcomes (daemon-client.test.ts:33-124).
Reason: “the first routing decision must prevent every later side effect” — PR body, Decisions #2; spec “Guard-List Admission and Routing”
open Routing spoke ↓
K9STATEDClient owns warm result capture and failure bytes
Package builds a DaemonClientResultCapture (OS temp dir) per warm request. Only a retry-safe transport failure reruns locally; uncertain acceptance or failed completion returns a warm failure. 5 failure codes → 3 “Cannot answer: …” messages, now defined in package and CLI. Malformed warm output is disposed before replacement; dispatcher did not.
Reason: “warm transfer cleanup and replay safety belong to the daemon client” — PR body, Decisions #4

K15STATEDKeep acceptance-based idle timing
The 30-minute idle deadline starts at construction and resets on navigation acceptance, not completion. Navigation that reaches its deadline triggers shutdown when the queue empties; a new test pins this. The functional spec excludes warm-up from idle, but this PR defers readiness-armed and completion-based timing; follow-ups grow from 6 to 8 items.
Reason: “readiness- and completion-based lifetime changes are explicitly deferred behavior” — PR body, Decisions #5

Skip to decisions
07
SYMNAV / DAEMON REFACTOR
Experiment notes ↗
26 moves.
One change of owner.

The daemon moves out of the CLI. Core retains workspaces; TypeScript keeps language rules. The running CLI switches in the last PR.

Lossy opening: “moving rooms” stands for both extracting responsibilities and relocating code. Most of the stack builds boundaries before crossing the package boundary.

01 / #123–128
Retain in core
Source bytes, revision publication, project membership, one-turn caches, and workspace sessions leave language or CLI ownership.
02 / #129–136
Name the boundaries
CLI resolves environment and injects execution. Daemon owns policy, command/failure/admission contracts. Renderer owns lifecycle bytes.
03 / #137–143
Split the transport
Framing, durable receipt, sockets, bounded exchanges, and accepted recovery acquire distinct owners inside the CLI.
04 / #144–147
Split the process
Activity projection, worker generations, delivery, and FIFO accepted turns separate. Ledger and spool keep their data.
05 / #148–149
Stage, then switch
Package mechanisms and DaemonClient coexist with active CLI copies for one PR. The final PR switches the host and removes copies.

The daemon is already warm-capable. The stack changes who owns its mechanisms, reusable state, contracts, and output. Follow the 26 stops to see each choice and its recorded reason, including accompanying test and documentation changes.

Start with source caching →
A LINEAR READING, WITH EXITS
Every move, in one place.
26 PRs · 5 chapters

These summaries carry the architectural and accompanying choices before any source drawer opens. Choose a move to see all its recorded decisions, the mechanism, and the same revision’s evidence.

RETAIN IN CORE · #123–128
#123
Move bytes, keep replacement behavior.
Source caching moves from TypeScript to core. A selected snapshot still evicts omitted cached bytes; selection-aware retention is deferred. The PR also rewrites the repository PR template without a recorded bundling reason.
↗
#124
Prepare a candidate; publish only after validation.
Core takes revision diffs and portable indexes. TypeScript keeps its mutation journal and exact source handles. Missing-file preparation still commits one file at a time.
↗
#126
Make project membership one publication.
Core discovers, observes, validates, and publishes project membership. TypeScript keeps tsconfig and toolchain hooks; FIFO order, inferred fallback, and release order remain explicit choices.
↗
#127
Keep six caches. Give them one lifetime.
Core owns clearing, while TypeScript keeps query algorithms, keys, and identities. Clear after successful refresh and synchronously before awaiting release; cached undefined still counts as a hit.
↗
#128
Warm means keeping the same core object.
Core sessions own discovery and backend lifetime. Cold runs use request discovery, warm runs retain a catalog, selections discover afresh, each turn gets a router, and release can be repeated.
↗
NAME THE BOUNDARIES · #129–136
#129
Resolve the environment once, in the host.
State-directory resolution moves from telemetry to CLI. One canonical path feeds both consumers, including paths with missing tails. Fixture synchronization and larger status-test budgets also land here.
↗
#130
Create the package before moving its mechanisms.
A dependency-free daemon package owns portable contracts and an immutable, complete policy snapshot. Limits, memory recipes, test overrides, and intentional missing deadlines get a policy record. Mechanisms still live in CLI.
↗
#131
The snapshot becomes the only threshold input.
Consumers require policy slices. Status has 100 ms while ordinary lifecycle exchanges have 250 ms. Fetch resumes and accepted reattachments use separate counters; test adapters replace production override seams.
↗
#132
Classify argv once. Carry the name.
CLI syntax selects one daemon-owned command identity beside opaque argv. It participates in duplicate compatibility. Protocol generation changes from 4 to 5, with mixed generations taking compatibility handling before execution.
↗
#133
One outer failure vocabulary; a separate worker domain.
Daemon owns outer failure codes, validation, and precedence. CLI supplies instanceof facts; worker failures keep their distinct wire values. Accepted terminal failures keep controlled results without local replay.
↗
#134
The first failed guard owns the answer.
Authentication, readiness, pressure, draining, and duplicate compatibility are ordered. Authentication failure disconnects; retry safety comes from the rejection code, and conflicting duplicates do not mutate accepted state.
↗
#135
The worker loads its host through a module URL.
CLI implements a daemon-defined executor contract. A validated absolute URL crosses process and worker boundaries. Worker code owns sequencing, rechunking, and sampling; diagnostics remain opaque. Two test budgets become 15 s.
↗
#136
Move output bytes to the renderer.
One stateless renderer formats public daemon start/status/stop reports. CLI still chooses format, writes output, and wraps errors. Renderer imports the daemon public reports.
↗
SPLIT THE TRANSPORT · #137–143
#137
Cut framing out of the transport facade.
Operation-shaped ports replace broad concrete dependencies. Codec and validator own binary framing, integrity, and frame-kind limits; facade mapping preserves transport error meaning.
↗
#138
A connection can end before a transfer does.
One receiver retains manifest, digest, and durable offsets across reconnections. Capture owns stored output; offsets advance only after append. Decoders are fresh per socket and output disposal transfers to the caller. A test budget grows 20→60 s.
↗
#139
Give every outbound exchange one byte connection.
A socket client owns connection timeout, pull-driven reads, FIFO writes, backpressure, and closure. The facade still interprets protocol and delivery state; inbound serving waits for its own step.
↗
#140
Group bounded responses by their shared lifecycle.
Lifecycle, execution-status, and result acknowledgement use one client for correlation, deadlines, and cleanup. Acknowledgement stays off the general lifecycle port; semantic validation precedes accepted classification.
↗
#141
Split the other side of the socket.
A server owns endpoint probes, listening, per-connection response/write chains, and shutdown. It reuses the socket client for probes; concurrent shutdown callers share settlement and force can escalate a drain.
↗
#142
Recover delivery without replaying accepted work.
A dedicated execution client owns admission through acknowledgement. Fetch resumes reuse an attempt’s receiver; identical-request reattachments create a new capture. Numeric budgets remain independent and exhausted fetches retain accepted-corruption meaning.
↗
#143
Leave the transport facade with only wiring.
One required policy composes the split owners. Direct component injection preserves returned identity; the canFrame probe disappears. A source-boundary test replaces any temptation to use file length as an architecture rule.
↗
SPLIT THE PROCESS · #144–147
#144
Capture state here; project it there.
A pure activity projector consumes explicit process, clock, queue, resource, and worker snapshots. It uses the in-progress worker generation and sampled spool bytes, keeps legacy fileCount behavior, and returns frozen values.
↗
#145
One manager owns each generation handoff.
Worker startup, execution, replacement, fencing, release, and shutdown move behind a manager. Resource policy stays behind a recovery port. Warm-up sampling gates readiness; replacement is shared, while force can interrupt graceful close.
↗
#146
Coordinate delivery without taking its data.
One delivery session coordinates attachment, transfer, acknowledgement, and traces. Ledger and spool keep state and bytes. The latest delivery is the queue barrier; expired traces are fenced, and cleanup failure does not withhold protocol acknowledgement.
↗
#147
Serialize accepted turns over existing owners.
An execution session coordinates the FIFO queue, delivery, worker, resources, and lifetime. Immutable metadata stays on ledger entries; sampling gates the next turn. Duplicates attach without a second acceptance or lifetime reset.
↗
STAGE, THEN SWITCH · #148–149
#148
Two copies exist. The CLI still runs its old graph.
DaemonClient, executable entries, and mechanisms arrive in the package. Its Node-free facade loads a private runtime; lazy routing stops at the first decision. CLI compatibility copies stay active while mechanism tests move. Clocks, registry authority, output ownership, and existing idle timing remain explicit.
↗
#149
Switch the caller. Delete the compatibility graph.
CLI invocation coordination calls DaemonClient and package transport composition replaces the old facade. External tests use a read-only inspector and package actors; syntax-aware rules enforce imports, clocks, exports, and storage. Policy serialization becomes private. Ten CLI status/stop scenarios disappear, pressure assertions change, and inspector failure handling is added.
↗

text:
rich-review / 08
131 · policy
148 · ownership
Evidence & method
ADVERSARIAL · READ ONLY

WORST HONEST READING / TWO REAL REFACTORS

The claim
has edges.

A refactor can keep the assertion, move the test, and change what the human thinks was preserved.

The promised invariant: the same inputs should produce the same output, execution mode, lifecycle outcome and failure behavior.

Read the changed boundary together with the evidence that constrains it. Neither a dramatic diff nor a passing test name tells the whole story.

No verdicts or stored responses. The questions are for the reader to carry into review.

131 · ORIENTATION
One policy reaches three places.
Required slices replace local defaults and numeric overrides.
@symnav/daemon · existing policy
complete, validated snapshot
↓ required values · newly consumed
Caller process
capture · socket
lifecycle composition
Daemon process
spool · resources
lifetime · diagnostics
Worker thread
chunk validation
heap sampling
Test adapters translate old knobs into valid policies → some disk stimuli become inline.

Grouped configuration map. The mechanisms are still in apps/cli at this head; unchanged interactions are omitted.

148 · ORIENTATION
Two graphs coexist at this head.
The package is staged; the shipped CLI keeps its local path.

apps/cli · shipped

CLI host
↓ local imports
38 compatibility files
process / worker / transport
execution / storage / lifecycle
↑ hash + CLI-facing tests

packages/daemon · staged

DaemonClient + entries
↓ private imports
Package mechanisms
no internal package dependency
↑ 37 relocated test files
The local graph changes before the freeze, including stricter ownership checks.

Grouped static/test map. The two columns are code graphs, not two daemons running together.

01 / STIMULUS
Same cleanup assertion; fifteen existing cases stop entering a spill path. Other disk tests remain.
02 / SCOPE
A recovery error and a synthetic lock-ownership outcome change. Each observation has a narrow, recorded input.
03 / REACH
Package tests and the shipped CLI now reach different copies. The new hash freezes the chosen local head.

Stated / unexplained refers to the reason, not correctness. Stated reasons come from the PR body or supplied specs/commits. Unexplained means no reason found for that exact choice in those materials.

Beyond the promise marks an observed difference that the unchanged-behavior contract did not request. It does not claim to know the author’s motives or that the change is undesirable.

The complete reading layer is below. Every record exposes its decisions, hardest fair reading and counterevidence. Open a mechanism for more fidelity on those same facts; use the numbered links to jump and return.

131

DECISION RECORD · 5 CONNECTED READINGS

Route daemon thresholds through centralized policy

The ownership move is broad. The important qualifications are narrow: separate timeout purposes, existing retry scopes, changed error provenance, and test adapters that change the input to the assertion.

b3a6c4fa5d → b100221db4
60 files · +1,298 / −544
01 Policy ownership
02 Deadlines & attempts
03 Failure identity
04 Test stimuli
05 Test replacements
01
PR 131
The snapshot becomes the source of the limits.
One policy
existing package snapshot
→
3 places
caller · daemon · worker

What moves: the source of thresholds. The CLI still owns these mechanisms at this head.

STATED Require output, resource, startup, shutdown, transport, delivery and diagnostic sections so omitted inputs cannot recreate local defaults.
STATED Feed the same resource values into reporting, supervision and worker limits; remove the local memory derivation.
STATED Route chunking, inline/result/aggregate capacity, framing, logs and trace retention through their policy owners. Preserve defaults and the absence of an accepted-completion deadline.

WORST HONEST READING
A change to one policy now reaches storage, transport validation and worker output together. “One owner” reduces scattered defaults but increases the number of consumers affected by a policy edit.

WHAT LIMITS THAT READING
The snapshot and its default/validation tests already exist in the base. This PR wires consumers to it; it does not introduce user tuning or move the mechanisms into the package.

Which consumers must change together when an output limit changes?
Inspect the mechanism and sources
01
02
PR 131
Equal-looking waits and retries keep separate owners.
100 ms
status observation
250 ms
ordinary one-response
5 s
execute admission

These waits are different purposes. Accepted completion has no timer.

STATED Select the short status timeout at composition, because a status observer and an execution-status exchange have different deadlines.
STATED Replace startup’s fixed retry and delivery’s fixed/boolean allowances with numeric policy budgets. Keep reattachment separate from fetch-resume allowance per execute attempt.
STATED Keep authorization, readiness observation, stop escalation, process-exit polling, acknowledgement drain and diagnostic retention independently configurable in tests.

WORST HONEST READING
The new field names can suggest that the base shared one retry budget. It did not: fetch state already lived inside executeOnce, and reattachment lived outside. Numeric representation and its loop rewrite are the changes.

WHAT LIMITS THAT READING
Default limits remain one startup retry, one post-accept reattachment and one fetch resume per execute attempt. Tests distinguish the two timeout fields with opposite overrides; their 100/250 ms defaults are pinned by the policy test. A recorded reattach-then-fetch succeeds in both versions.

Can a composition call accidentally turn an ordinary exchange into the short status observer?
Inspect the mechanism and sources
02
03
PR 131
Recovery now decides which failure survives.
close
first accepted stream
→
corrupt
accepted reattachment

Recorded result: base → closed; head → corrupt. Two execute submissions in both.

Ranking. First, a promise whose evidence changed; then a boundary whose ownership changed; then a missing rationale. This is an ordering of questions, not a correctness score.

DIFF OF INTENT · TWO LAYERS OF ONE REFACTOR

Follow the promise.

A plan names the destination. A PR names a step. The code makes the step concrete.

HOW TO READ THE FIGURES

Right: the implemented boundary.

scope distinction or extra choice

Two moves, two scales.

READ-ONLY STUDY

+
The shared plan preserves failure paths. The PR explains numeric retry budgets, but says nothing about choosing a different failure to return.

the stated reason

the stated reason

10
Legacy test knobs move behind test-only adapters
+
Keep small test thresholds without restoring compatibility overloads in production.
direct trace
Seven helper files wrap runtime APIs with policy-backed defaults and overrides. Unit, integration, e2e, cleanup, and benchmark callers change imports.
REASON STATED
The PR explicitly chooses test-only adapters because tests need small thresholds and runtime tuning seams must not return.
11
Resource derivation tests leave the CLI suite
+
The plan says preserve daemon expectations. The PR’s tree describes test adaptations and preserved threshold behavior.
test contract
The old five-row derivation table, constrained-memory case, and constant-cadence case are deleted. Related policy tests already existed in the base; the 256 MiB row is not copied exactly.
REASON UNEXPLAINED
The removed class explains the structural context, but no reviewed source states a reason for deleting these particular tests. Existing library coverage is evidence, not an invented rationale.
12
Tests change input values and record shapes
+
Adapt legacy knobs to validated policies. The existing validator requires 0 < chunk ≤ inline ≤ result ≤ aggregate.
test contract
Spill points and chunk boundaries change: local capture uses 32 instead of 1 byte; zero-inline cases now cross a positive boundary; “xx” becomes two records. One helper accepts memoryCapBytes without applying it.
REASON UNEXPLAINED
The adapter strategy has a stated reason, but these exact transformations and the unused legacy memoryCapBytes field are not explained in the reviewed sources.

Tests probe injected values and ban retired names
+
Prevent local defaults from returning and preserve threshold/retry behavior at the consumer boundary.
test contract
Added tests inject distinctive caps, timings, queue size, and startup retry counts; one delivery test nests fetch under reattachment. The meta-test expands its retired-string scan.
REASON STATED
The PR describes test files as preserving thresholds/retries and the meta-test as rejecting retired defaults and bypasses.

↑ Back to both subjects
END OF #131 MAP

READING KEY AND LIMITS

Intent is a source, not a time machine.
Stated / unexplained

Stated means a reason or purpose exists in the supplied body, commit messages, or reviewed plans. Unexplained means those sources disclose no reason for that choice. It does not mean the choice is wrong or unauthorized.

Plan / body / code

The shared architecture plan describes the whole stack. These pages compare only each subject’s own base and head. A PR body may have been written after the code; this is a contract comparison, not proof of what was requested first.

Evidence / execution

Both patches were read. Sources and test assertions are available offline at exact revisions. A focused source probe checks cache behavior and reattachment error selection. No full suite or end-to-end parity result is claimed.

No implementation transcript or phase-specific plan was supplied in either bundle. Commit bodies are empty. Overview files contain path headings rather than usable symbol output. Earlier experiments were not read.

Preserve semantic query failure behavior and promise identity.
direct trace
A returned promise stays cached after rejection. A synchronous factory throw leaves the slot empty. Old promises can settle after a clear without replacing new entries.
REASON STATED
The body makes preservation the constraint; the added characterization tests specify these two failure paths.

04
A turn starts after a successful refresh
+
Do not clear at refresh entry: failed refresh must preserve the current successful turn.
direct trace
Source/project/state refresh runs first. Only after the awaited refresh succeeds does the backend call beginTurn and clear every handle.
REASON STATED
The PR explicitly gives failed-refresh preservation as the reason for this ordering.

05
Release becomes an awaited boundary
+
Clear synchronously before project release. The PR explicitly adds an awaited backend release barrier.
scope needs
distinguishing
Cache entries disappear first. Service and backend wait for project release and carry its rejection to the caller. Queries can refill a handle while release is pending.
REASON STATED
The PR says released semantics must be unavailable while release is pending or rejecting. Clearing removes old entries; it does not disable queries.

06
The concrete API is a composed scope
+
The shared plan describes core bases that backends extend. The PR lists a standalone scope and a narrower beginTurn input.
choice beyond
the stated reason
The service instantiates the scope rather than inheriting it. beginTurn takes only files. Core exports the scope and a getOrCreate-only handle.
REASON UNEXPLAINED
The API is disclosed, but the reviewed sources give no reason for composition versus inheritance or for narrowing snapshot to files.

07
Release clears values, not the handles
+
The public API names beginTurn and releaseTransientResources; it has no handle disposal method.
choice beyond
the stated reason
The scope retains its handle registry. Both lifecycle calls clear the same maps; repeated release and later reuse remain possible.
REASON UNEXPLAINED
The implementation and tests make this lifetime concrete. No reason is given for retaining every registered handle or omitting a terminal released state.

08
Ten added cases expose the preservation contract
+
Characterize TypeScript cache behavior and lock identity, failure, and clearing contracts.
test contract
Six service cases and four core cases are added. Existing cases and assertions remain; release ordering and failed refresh gain explicit checks.
REASON STATED
The PR’s file tree names characterization and contract locking as the purposes of these test changes.
Later completion errors can replace the original error.

01
Policy crosses into existing CLI mechanisms
+
The snapshot already crosses processes. This PR makes operational consumers receive required policy sections; package extraction is the wider plan.
scope needs
distinguishing
Constructor defaults and optional threshold inputs are replaced by required slices. Daemon mechanisms remain in apps/cli. No packages/daemon file changes.
REASON STATED
The PR says omitted composition must not recreate local defaults. Its before/after diagrams keep the mechanisms in the CLI.

02
Memory policy stops being re-derived by consumers
+
Resource supervision consumes the snapshot’s resource section, including limits and sampling/replacement policy.
direct trace
The CLI resource-policy class is deleted. Workspace reporting, worker heap limits, pressure thresholds, two sampling cadences, and replacement budgets read the same section.
REASON STATED
One owner and preserved resource behavior are stated in the PR and policy record; the record gives reasons for the individual thresholds.

03
One output policy follows bytes end to end
+
Capture, spooling, framing, and worker validation use required output/resource policy inputs.
direct trace
Chunk, inline, per-result, aggregate spool, JSON, and execution-control capacities reach their consumers. File decoding and both worker-message ends receive the chunk cap.
REASON STATED
Required inputs prevent fallback defaults; the policy record separately explains the six byte limits.

04
Lifecycle intervals stay separate
+
Use required startup and shutdown policy; preserve independent cadences and the deliberate absence of a healthy-startup deadline.
direct trace
Election grace, heartbeat, authorization, observation, child retries, idle lifetime, stop escalation, signals, and drain acknowledgements read distinct fields. An unused startup timeout option disappears.
REASON STATED
The policy record explains each timing and explicitly says progressing warm-up has no project-size deadline.

05
Logs and traces inherit their own budgets
+
Logging, rotation, and disconnected trace retention use the required diagnostic section.
direct trace
Log size, backup count, queued events, trace expiry, and retained-trace capacity read policy. The effective minimum of one retained trace remains.
REASON STATED
The policy record gives bounded storage/history and reconnect evidence as the reasons, and records the effective minimum of one.

06
The caller’s purpose chooses the timeout
+
Status observation gets 100 ms. Ordinary lifecycle and execution-status exchanges keep 250 ms. Execute admission has its own 5 s timer.
direct trace
The status command composes a status-observer transport. The constructor selects that deadline for its requests; ordinary construction selects the other deadline. Acceptance disables the admission timer.
REASON STATED
The PR explicitly distinguishes status observation from ordinary execution-status requests; the policy record keeps accepted completion untimed.

07
Recovery budgets have two nesting levels
+
Use independent numeric reattachment and fetch-resume budgets; each reattached execute attempt gets its own fetch allowance.
scope needs
distinguishing
An outer counter limits accepted-execution reattachments. A counter inside each executeOnce limits fetch starts. Both default to one; a fetch failure still ends that attempt.
REASON STATED
The PR gives per-attempt fetch allowance as the reason for separate counters. The policy record describes one fetch resume per execute attempt.

08
A later completion error can become the caller’s error
+
The shared plan preserves failure paths. The PR explains numeric retry budgets, but says nothing about choosing a different failure to return.
choice beyond
the stated reason
If the reattached submission fails, both versions return the first error. If it is accepted and its completion fails, the head can return that later error; the base returned the first.
REASON UNEXPLAINED
No reason for the changed error selection was found in the body, commit messages, or reviewed plans. This is a concrete delta beyond the stated counter rationale.

09
Some numeric seams remain inside production APIs
+
Replace optional per-consumer numbers so runtime consumers cannot bypass the snapshot.
choice beyond
the stated reason
Registry grace still accepts an explicit numeric argument. Transport still accepts writeChunkSize. Codecs take required numeric caps; callers in this layer supply policy values.
REASON UNEXPLAINED
No reason was found for retaining the optional grace and write-fragmentation inputs. Both predate this PR; neither is a new user-facing tuning option.

10
Legacy test knobs move behind test-only adapters
+
Keep small test thresholds without restoring compatibility overloads in production.
direct trace
Seven helper files wrap runtime APIs with policy-backed defaults and overrides. Unit, integration, e2e, cleanup, and benchmark callers change imports.
REASON STATED
The PR explicitly chooses test-only adapters because tests need small thresholds and runtime tuning seams must not return.

11
Resource derivation tests leave the CLI suite
+
The plan says preserve daemon expectations. The PR’s tree describes test adaptations and preserved threshold behavior.
test contract
The old five-row derivation table, constrained-memory case, and constant-cadence case are deleted. Related policy tests already existed in the base; the 256 MiB row is not copied exactly.
REASON UNEXPLAINED
The removed class explains the structural context, but no reviewed source states a reason for deleting these particular tests. Existing library coverage is evidence, not an invented rationale.

12
Tests change input values and record shapes
+
Adapt legacy knobs to validated policies. The existing validator requires 0 < chunk ≤ inline ≤ result ≤ aggregate.
test contract
Spill points and chunk boundaries change: local capture uses 32 instead of 1 byte; zero-inline cases now cross a positive boundary; “xx” becomes two records. One helper accepts memoryCapBytes without applying it.
REASON UNEXPLAINED
The adapter strategy has a stated reason, but these exact transformations and the unused legacy memoryCapBytes field are not explained in the reviewed sources.

13
Tests probe injected values and ban retired names
+
Prevent local defaults from returning and preserve threshold/retry behavior at the consumer boundary.
test contract
Added tests inject distinctive caps, timings, queue size, and startup retry counts; one delivery test nests fetch under reattachment. The meta-test expands its retired-string scan.
REASON STATED
The PR describes test files as preserving thresholds/retries and the meta-test as rejecting retired defaults and bypasses.

name: 11-chess-coach
title: Chess coach · PR 131
text:
Skip to the decisions
♞
CHESS COACH
/ 11
Position
22 moves
Analysis
Evidence
SYMNAV · PR 131 · PART 08 OF THE DAEMON REFACTOR
The number stays.
The authority moves.

One policy already crosses the process boundaries. This change makes the mechanisms use it—and closes many of their old tuning inputs.

THE COACH’S LENS

See the move played beside the move left on the board. Learn what each commits you to.

Chess is a lossy analogy here. These are design alternatives, not legal chess moves or grades.
01–04
Who supplies the limits?
05–15
Which clock, budget, or retention rule?
16–22
What did the test and API changes mean?

The full decision layer is the move sheet below. It includes test deletions, changed fixtures and details the PR does not explain. Every deeper panel elaborates one of those same decisions.

THE POSITION
Move a boundary, keep the pieces in place.
Base position
Played position
PACKAGES/DAEMON · ALREADY IN THE BASE
DaemonPolicy
One complete snapshot
resources · output · transport · delivery
startup · shutdown · diagnostics
required inputs ↓
APPS/CLI · IMPLEMENTATIONS REMAIN HERE
Composition
Program / commands / dispatcher / process & worker entries
projects policy values →
Local threshold ownership removed from these constructors
Resource supervisor
RSS, replacement circuit
Output / spool / codecs
chunks, storage, frames
Transport
deadlines, recovery
Lifecycle / diagnostics
startup, stop, idle, logs
Test boundary
Legacy knobs → test adapters → validated policy
Fixture meanings change too ↗

Solid teal marks the policy inputs made required by this PR. The package containing each mechanism does not move. Some helper functions still take scalar values.

THE SAME CHANGE THROUGH THE RUNTIME LENS
CLI PROCESS
Create policy from memory
Compose controller + transport
Capture local command output
serialized
snapshot →
DAEMON PROCESS
Consume received values
Registry · spool · resource supervisor
Lifetime · logger · transport
serialized
snapshot →
WORKER THREAD
Consume received values
V8 heap · heap sampling
Command capture · chunk validation

Snapshot transfer already exists in the base. New consumption is inside the boxes. Each process uses its local copy; the worker returns output chunks through the daemon’s spool and socket to the client.

THE COMPLETE DECISION LAYER
22 moves. The alternatives stay visible.
Read the analysis in order ↓

STATED A reason exists in the PR or policy record. UNEXPLAINED No reason found for this specific choice.

Alternative named in PR is the author’s contrast. Base behavior is checked source. Coach’s variation is hypothetical. Consequences and questions are the coach’s reading, not invented author intent.

DECISION
MOVE PLAYED
MOVE NOT PLAYED
Who owns the position?
01
Make composition obligatory
STATED
PLAYED

Required policy sections enter each mechanism.

ALTERNATIVE NAMED IN PR

Keep optional numbers and local fallback defaults.

A missing policy input becomes a missing constructor argument; clocks, storage, paths and worker injection remain separate dependencies.

CLI constructors change; the policy package and its snapshot already exist. Mechanisms stay in apps/cli in this PR.

Reason on record: The PR says omitted composition must not recreate local defaults.

Analyze 01 ↗
Who owns the position?
02
Use the resource snapshot verbatim
STATED
PLAYED

Supervisor, ready record and worker heap use policy.resources.

BASE BEHAVIOR

Re-derive resources from effective memory or a separate memory cap.

The hard cap reported at readiness and the worker heap limit now come from the same supplied values. The CLI resource-policy class is deleted.

RSS hard / soft / resume limits; raw effective memory; V8 heap limit; 250 ms supervision; two replacements in ten minutes, then drain.

Reason on record: The policy record requires one complete snapshot across process and worker boundaries; the architecture spec gives thresholds one owner.

Analyze 02 ↗
Who owns the position?
03
Carry the output limits all the way through
STATED
PLAYED

Capture, spool, disk decode and both worker endpoints share output limits.

BASE BEHAVIOR

Give each output stage its own constants and optional capacities.

A record accepted by one stage is checked against the same chunk limit at later stages. Local CLI execution also consumes the output section.

64 KiB raw chunks → 256 KiB inline → 256 MiB per result → 512 MiB aggregate spool. These are existing defaults, not new tuning.

Reason on record: The PR explicitly routes output capture, spooling and worker validation through required output slices; the record states why each bound exists.

Analyze 03 ↗
Who owns the position?
04
Keep three framing capacities distinct
STATED
PLAYED

Ordinary JSON, execution control and raw binary chunks keep separate bounds.

COACH’S VARIATION · HYPOTHETICAL

Use one frame-size limit for all traffic.

The transfer decoder allows a binary envelope of control capacity plus chunk capacity; the codec separately checks raw chunk length. Socket write fragmentation remains an option.

8 MiB JSON; 256 KiB execution control; 64 KiB raw chunk. Numeric codec arguments replace imports of spool-owned constants.

Reason on record: The policy record distinguishes decoded control input, binary-transfer control and one raw record.

Analyze 04 ↗
Which clock is running?
05
Choose the timeout by caller purpose
STATED
PLAYED

Status observer: 100 ms. Ordinary transport: 250 ms.

ALTERNATIVE NAMED IN PR

Choose a timeout from the request’s kind.

The same identify or ping message can serve different callers. An execution-status request still uses the ordinary timeout; the word “status” does not select 100 ms.

The CLI status action sets responseTimeoutPurpose: status-observer. Ordinary is the default purpose. The constructor selects the value once.

Reason on record: The PR says status observation and ordinary execution-status requests have distinct deadlines.

Analyze 05 ↗
Which clock is running?
06
End the execution timer at acceptance
STATED
PLAYED

Policy supplies the 5 s admission timer; acceptance disables it.

COACH’S VARIATION · HYPOTHETICAL

Carry that timer into command completion.

Long accepted work keeps running without a completion deadline. Fetch and worker-output acknowledgement also retain their existing absence of a timer.

This is preserved behavior while the timer’s source changes. Healthy startup and unacknowledged-result retention likewise have no new expiry.

Reason on record: The policy record bounds admission without timing accepted completion; accepted work must not be replayed or failed for running long.

Analyze 06 ↗
How many chances remain?
07
Give recovery two independent budgets
STATED
PLAYED

Count execute reattachments outside; count fetch resumes inside each execute attempt.

ALTERNATIVE NAMED IN PR

Share a single used-retry flag across both recovery scopes.

A reattached execute attempt receives a fresh fetch allowance. Reattachment resends the same request identity after an authenticated accepted close; this is recovery, not local replay.

Default: one reattachment and one fetch resume per attempt. Base already nested the two scopes; this PR replaces fixed one-shot control with policy numbers. Added trace: execute → reattach → fetch.

Reason on record: The PR says every reattached execute attempt has its own fetch-resume allowance.

Analyze 07 ↗
How many chances remain?
08
Let the latest completion error escape
UNEXPLAINED
PLAYED

A later accepted completion failure is caught in the next loop iteration.

BASE BEHAVIOR

Always preserve the original accepted-close error.

When reattachment is accepted and its completion fails, the exposed error can now be that later failure. A failure before reattachment acceptance still rethrows the preceding error.

An effect of the numeric loop rewrite, separate from the stated reason for independent counters. No correctness verdict is attached.

Reason not found: No reason for this error-selection change was found in the PR, six commit messages, policy record or architecture spec.

Analyze 08 ↗
How many chances remain?
09
Keep the fetch path as one connection
UNEXPLAINED
PLAYED

Read a numeric resume allowance at the original execute socket; fetch itself has no retry loop.

COACH’S VARIATION · HYPOTHETICAL

Retry failed fetch connections until that numeric allowance is spent.

The code distinguishes an allowance from a complete repeated-fetch mechanism. Fetch failure rejects this attempt. The new reattachment test makes one fetch; it does not demonstrate repeated fetch failures with a limit above one.

Default limit is one. The limit check lives in executeOnce.resume(); fetchCompletion().catch(fail) exits the attempt. Outer recovery still has its own eligibility checks.

Reason not found: The PR explains independent counters, but does not explain retaining one fetch connection while accepting a numeric resume limit.

Analyze 09 ↗
Which clock is running?
10
Separate election grace from healthy warm-up
STATED
PLAYED

Use 15 s coordination grace for ownership; leave healthy readiness waiting unbounded.

COACH’S VARIATION · HYPOTHETICAL

Use “startup timeout” as one wall-clock deadline for every startup phase.

Registry ownership, daemon authorization and missing-owner observation consume the grace. A progressing warm-up does not expire because a large project takes time.

The unused startupTimeoutMs field is removed; the active grace is named coordinationGraceMs. Grace still has a scalar override on a registry helper (move 21).

Reason on record: The policy record preserves election recovery grace and explicitly gives progressing warm-up no project-size deadline.

Analyze 10 ↗
How many chances remain?
11
Count failed child launches explicitly
STATED
PLAYED

A local failure counter permits the configured number of fresh startup tries.

BASE BEHAVIOR

Use a hard-coded catch-and-try-once branch.

Only child exit or lost warm-up consumes this recovery route. Waiting for another owner does not reset the budget. Default one retry is preserved; tests exercise zero and two.

Retry limit counts retries after the first try: zero → one launch, two → up to three launches in the added tests.

Reason on record: The policy record preserves one fresh launch after a failed child; the PR routes retry behavior through numeric policy.

Analyze 11 ↗
Which clock is running?
12
Keep each cadence attached to its job
STATED
PLAYED

Wire separate policy leaves into heartbeat, authorization, observation and worker sampling.

COACH’S VARIATION · HYPOTHETICAL

Use one generic polling interval.

Equal or nearby intervals remain independently named. Worker sampling receives a projected number; process entries continue to receive the complete serialized snapshot.

100 ms heartbeat; 10 ms authorization; 20 ms readiness observation; 25 ms worker heap sampling; 250 ms RSS supervision (move 02).

Reason on record: The record preserves distinct authorization and observation cadences, live startup ownership and short-lived heap-peak observation.

Analyze 12 ↗
Which clock is running?
13
Preserve the shutdown time budget’s parts
STATED
PLAYED

Stop, escalation reserve, signal waits and acknowledgement polling use distinct leaves.

COACH’S VARIATION · HYPOTHETICAL

Collapse shutdown waits into one shared timeout.

A stop still reserves min(500 ms, floor(stop timeout / 2)) for force termination. Each process signal has its own bounded exit interval; completion acknowledgement has a separate drain grace.

5 s stop; 500 ms maximum reserve; 20 ms controller polling; 500 ms per SIGTERM/SIGKILL exit wait; 20 ms exit polling; 250 ms drain acknowledgement at 5 ms intervals.

Reason on record: The record states bounded stop escalation, preservation of small stop windows and an opportunity for attached clients to acknowledge.

Supply a free-standing number or use the CLI’s exported idle constant.

Thirty-minute idle lifetime keeps its existing navigation semantics: accepted navigation and the queue becoming idle control the timer; an active navigation is allowed to finish.

A Pick of one shutdown leaf is enough for this consumer. The class keeps its timer and callback; only threshold ownership changes.

Use trace expiry or log capacity to decide whether completed output survives.

Log rotation and queue size are policy inputs. Trace expiry discards diagnostic state, not the completion spool; trace capacity retains an effective minimum of one.

10 MiB active-log rotation; four backups; 1,024 queued events; five-minute disconnected traces; 1,024 traces with max(1, value). Logger queue overflow test is added.

Reason on record: The record bounds diagnostic memory/history and retains reconnect evidence without changing result retention; result eviction is deferred.

Helpers cover controller, process terminator, registry, resource policy, startup coordinator, local transport and workspace daemon. Test factory validates by the existing serialized-policy codec.

FIELD NOTES / rich-review
CASE 148 · EXPERIMENT 12
About this experiment ↗

DAEMON ARCHITECTURE · A CONTRIBUTOR’S SYMPTOM

The host
knew too much.

A host wants to run a command. Why must it know how to find, start, probe, and recover a daemon?

PR 148’S MOVE

Put those mechanisms behind DaemonClient in @symnav/daemon. The shipped CLI still uses its compatibility graph.

Symnav navigates TypeScript code. This stack changes ownership for contributors and hosts; unchanged user behavior is the requirement.

Reconstructed symptom · illustrative, not a captured bug report
REQUEST
“Run this command
in this workspace.”
To make that call, the CLI assembles…
registry
transport
terminator
launcher
observer
startup coordinator
Read the actual construction site ↗
The complete brief
→
Follow the clues
→
Inspect the sources

AT THE SCENE

Two paths exist at the head of this PR.
Before #148
At #148

The production route remains here.
CLI dispatcher + lifecycle registration
Host builds registry, transport, startup, launcher, observer, terminator
↓

CLI-local process entry and worker entry
38 frozen compatibility mechanism files
execution · delivery · registry · transport · worker · resources · lifetime · diagnostics

Dispatcher and lifecycle registration: byte-identical to the base. The mechanisms were prepared before the freeze.

PACKAGES/DAEMON · ADDED MECHANISM OWNERSHIP
A new host-facing path is available.
DaemonClient → private Node runtime
Host calls execute() or control(); no mechanism factories in its public contract
↓
Routing + lifecycle composition
guards · registry · transports · controller · startup
