THE COMPLETE BRIEF · STOP AFTER THIS LAYER IF YOU HAVE ENOUGH

Six clues. Twenty-four decisions.

STATED reason found
UNEXPLAINED reason for this choice not found

The architecture, preserved behaviors, deferrals, and test changes are all here. Each decision opens its reason and source; each clue opens a closer view. “Unexplained” records a missing rationale, not a correctness judgment.

01
The host knows too much ↗

Move the composition burden behind a public client.

D01
Give hosts execute and typed control reports
STATED

Hosts supply environment, executor factory + module URL, readiness probe, and classified requests. The client returns output + mode or a lifecycle report.

reason + evidence ↗
D02
Keep declarations free of Node types
STATED

The façade dynamically loads its Node runtime during construction. Portable declarations do not make execution browser-compatible.

reason + evidence ↗
D03
Package the process and worker around injected execution
STATED

The package owns executable entries and private mechanisms; the host executor still supplies product behavior. The daemon imports no other production symnav package.

reason + evidence ↗
02
The old route is still connected ↗

Ownership is staged before the consumer switches.

D04
Keep the shipped CLI on its compatibility graph
STATED

The dispatcher and lifecycle registration remain byte-identical to the base. This PR adds the package path; it does not switch those consumers.

reason + evidence ↗
D05
Freeze 38 app-local mechanism files
STATED

A path-and-content hash freezes the compatibility graph after preparation. It normalizes CRLF; dispatcher, route, and workspace selector are excluded.

reason + evidence ↗
D06
Group mechanisms by the concern they own
STATED

Client, process, registry, transport, execution, delivery, worker, resources, diagnostics, and lifecycle become package folders. The coordinator is renamed before copying.

reason + evidence ↗
03
The first answer ends the search ↗

Order determines which observations can happen.

D07
Use four ordered, lazy routing guards
STATED

Record present → not starting → version → responsive. Read and observation are memoized; a decision prevents every later guard and its effects.

reason + evidence ↗
D08
Keep the route and local-execution distinctions
STATED

Disabled, absent, starting, or recovering run cold; ready/busy run warm; dead/incompatible fall back. Only absent/fallback routing decisions trigger independent warmup. Local attempts get fresh executors. Errors and exact-process cleanup keep their distinct routes.

reason + evidence ↗
D09
Compose lifecycle once, with a separate status timeout
STATED

Disabled blocks start; status and stop still operate. The host supplies the readiness command, which still runs through execution. Control failures reject to the host wrapper.

reason + evidence ↗
04
A missing answer is not permission to replay ↗

The client owns the boundary between a retry and a second execution.

D10
Let transport retry-safety authorize fallback
STATED

A retry-safe warm submission failure gets one local fallback. An uncertain or accepted failure stays warm and produces a controlled failure instead of replay.

reason + evidence ↗
D11
Own warm output capture inside the package
STATED

Each transfer gets a fresh policy-limited capture, using memory then an OS-temporary spool. The returned output still has records() and dispose(); the host does not provide capture factories.

reason + evidence ↗
D12
Own failure output and malformed-result cleanup
STATED

Resource, response-capacity, and incomplete-request failures become stderr + exit 1. A missing output or non-integer exit code is incomplete; any available malformed output is disposed.

reason + evidence ↗
05
Who is allowed to act? ↗

Centralize authority while preserving the old timing and authentication rules.

D13
Validate adopted coordinates inside the coordinator
UNEXPLAINED

The renamed coordinator takes coordinates, a serving port, a workspace-exists callback, and an explicit clock. Identity mismatches fail before component setup; that placement has no stated rationale.

reason + evidence ↗
D14
Give registry startup equality one owner
STATED

Callers request named identity/instance/token/PID checks. One predicate compares the requested coordinates; exact-owner cleanup also compares timestamps and revision.

reason + evidence ↗
D15
Pin the existing authentication order and exceptions
UNEXPLAINED

Execution checks protocol/instance before token. Identify/terminate/kill use identity credentials; ping/stop still omit token checks. No reason for that asymmetry was found.

reason + evidence ↗
D16
Use a daemon-owned clock API
STATED

Daemon mechanisms stop using telemetry clocks and raw time sources. Wall time still owns persisted/lifetime deadlines; monotonic time owns elapsed execution and queue measurements.

reason + evidence ↗
D17
Defer readiness- and completion-based idle timing
STATED

Idle time starts in the constructor and resets at navigation acceptance. Long startup or a long completed turn can exhaust it. Ready/completion resets are written down as future behavior.

reason + evidence ↗
06
The witnesses changed too ↗

Test ownership is part of the extraction, with visible scope changes.

D18
Move 37 mechanism test files into the daemon package
STATED

Package tests use generic executor fixtures and local helpers, including standalone module fixtures and tsx tooling. CLI product behavior stays with CLI tests.

reason + evidence ↗
D19
Narrow the relocated worker test
UNEXPLAINED

Generic readiness replaces the CLI version scenario and drops startup/execution duration assertions. Version rejection returns as a direct CLI-factory test, losing the former worker-initialization assertion.

reason + evidence ↗
D20
Replace the mocked CLI entry tests with built-entry evidence
STATED

The CLI entry test file is deleted. New package tests exercise compiled worker, launcher, process initialization, and cleanup. They test a different boundary, not the same mock assertions.

reason + evidence ↗
D21
Retire policy-testing exports and their lint guard
UNEXPLAINED

The export map becomes root + two side-effect-only entries. Policy helpers move to test folders; the old import restriction and its positive/negative tests are deleted.

reason + evidence ↗
D22
Add a clock-ownership scan limited to one folder
UNEXPLAINED

The new test scans only siblings of lifecycle/daemon-clock.test.ts. Process, registry, worker, and execution folders are outside its scope.

reason + evidence ↗
D23
Disable parallel execution of package test files
UNEXPLAINED

The new Vitest configuration sets fileParallelism: false. No explanation accompanies this choice.

reason + evidence ↗
D24
Give Windows termination a different cleanup assertion
UNEXPLAINED

The built-process test permits a retained record and absent termination diagnostic on Windows, then has its caller remove the exited record. Other platforms expect process cleanup.

reason + evidence ↗

D01
Give hosts execute and typed control reports
STATED

Hosts supply environment, executor factory + module URL, readiness probe, and classified requests. The client returns output + mode or a lifecycle report.

D02
Keep declarations free of Node types
STATED

The façade dynamically loads its Node runtime during construction. Portable declarations do not make execution browser-compatible.

reason + evidence ↗

D03
Package the process and worker around injected execution
STATED

The package owns executable entries and private mechanisms; the host executor still supplies product behavior. The daemon imports no other production symnav package.

reason + evidence ↗
The old route is still connected ↗

D04
Keep the shipped CLI on its compatibility graph
STATED

The dispatcher and lifecycle registration remain byte-identical to the base. This PR adds the package path; it does not switch those consumers.

reason + evidence ↗

D05
Freeze 38 app-local mechanism files
STATED

A path-and-content hash freezes the compatibility graph after preparation. It normalizes CRLF; dispatcher, route, and workspace selector are excluded.

reason + evidence ↗

D06
Group mechanisms by the concern they own
STATED

Client, process, registry, transport, execution, delivery, worker, resources, diagnostics, and lifecycle become package folders. The coordinator is renamed before copying.

reason + evidence ↗
The first answer ends the search ↗

D07
Use four ordered, lazy routing guards
STATED

Record present → not starting → version → responsive. Read and observation are memoized; a decision prevents every later guard and its effects.

reason + evidence ↗

D08
Keep the route and local-execution distinctions
STATED

Disabled, absent, starting, or recovering run cold; ready/busy run warm; dead/incompatible fall back. Only absent/fallback routing decisions trigger independent warmup. Local attempts get fresh executors. Errors and exact-process cleanup keep their distinct routes.

reason + evidence ↗

D09
Compose lifecycle once, with a separate status timeout
STATED

Disabled blocks start; status and stop still operate. The host supplies the readiness command, which still runs through execution. Control failures reject to the host wrapper.

reason + evidence ↗
A missing answer is not permission to replay ↗

D10
Let transport retry-safety authorize fallback
STATED

A retry-safe warm submission failure gets one local fallback. An uncertain or accepted failure stays warm and produces a controlled failure instead of replay.

reason + evidence ↗

D11
Own warm output capture inside the package
STATED

Each transfer gets a fresh policy-limited capture, using memory then an OS-temporary spool. The returned output still has records() and dispose(); the host does not provide capture factories.

reason + evidence ↗

D12
Own failure output and malformed-result cleanup
STATED

Resource, response-capacity, and incomplete-request failures become stderr + exit 1. A missing output or non-integer exit code is incomplete; any available malformed output is disposed.

reason + evidence ↗

D13
Validate adopted coordinates inside the coordinator
UNEXPLAINED

The renamed coordinator takes coordinates, a serving port, a workspace-exists callback, and an explicit clock. Identity mismatches fail before component setup; that placement has no stated rationale.

reason + evidence ↗

D14
Give registry startup equality one owner
STATED

Callers request named identity/instance/token/PID checks. One predicate compares the requested coordinates; exact-owner cleanup also compares timestamps and revision.

reason + evidence ↗

D15
Pin the existing authentication order and exceptions
UNEXPLAINED

Execution checks protocol/instance before token. Identify/terminate/kill use identity credentials; ping/stop still omit token checks. No reason for that asymmetry was found.

reason + evidence ↗

D16
Use a daemon-owned clock API
STATED

Daemon mechanisms stop using telemetry clocks and raw time sources. Wall time still owns persisted/lifetime deadlines; monotonic time owns elapsed execution and queue measurements.

reason + evidence ↗

D17
Defer readiness- and completion-based idle timing
STATED

Idle time starts in the constructor and resets at navigation acceptance. Long startup or a long completed turn can exhaust it. Ready/completion resets are written down as future behavior.

reason + evidence ↗

D18
Move 37 mechanism test files into the daemon package
STATED

Package tests use generic executor fixtures and local helpers, including standalone module fixtures and tsx tooling. CLI product behavior stays with CLI tests.

reason + evidence ↗

Narrow the relocated worker test
UNEXPLAINED

Generic readiness replaces the CLI version scenario and drops startup/execution duration assertions. Version rejection returns as a direct CLI-factory test, losing the former worker-initialization assertion.

reason + evidence ↗

D20
Replace the mocked CLI entry tests with built-entry evidence
STATED

The CLI entry test file is deleted. New package tests exercise compiled worker, launcher, process initialization, and cleanup. They test a different boundary, not the same mock assertions.

Retire policy-testing exports and their lint guard
UNEXPLAINED

The export map becomes root + two side-effect-only entries. Policy helpers move to test folders; the old import restriction and its positive/negative tests are deleted.

UNEXPLAINED

The new test scans only siblings of lifecycle/daemon-clock.test.ts. Process, registry, worker, and execution folders are outside its scope.

UNEXPLAINED

The new Vitest configuration sets fileParallelism: false. No explanation accompanies this choice.

UNEXPLAINED

The built-process test permits a retained record and absent termination diagnostic on Windows, then has its caller remove the exited record. Other platforms expect process cleanup.

Teal border = responsibility received across a package boundary. The daemon package is new; core and renderer already existed.

Affected responsibilities only: the left-hand map omits existing core primitives and renderer work. “After” shows the responsibility transfers, not new runtime processes.

The daemon can load a supplied executor module at runtime. It does not import core or TypeScript as package dependencies. The public façade avoids Node ambient types; its dynamically loaded runtime still uses Node.

Locked dependency table ↗ Façade and lazy runtime ↗
Carry these six facts into every detail.
01 / STATE
Retain preparation; renew meaning.

Source bytes, file indexes, project membership, and a session live longer than one query. Six independent semantic caches clear on a successful new turn or before release. Publication is per backend index or project graph; there is no whole-pipeline transaction. Selection refresh still evicts omitted source bytes.

02 / HOST
The host knows the product.

The CLI classifies syntax, resolves the workspace and state path, supplies an absolute executor module URL, and writes output. The daemon owns routing and captures warm output. The renderer also formats lifecycle reports. Build rules enforce the final package surface.

03 / POLICY & IDENTITY
One owner for each rule.

Immutable policy sections cross process and worker boundaries. Values stay fixed for users. One command vocabulary, distinct failure vocabularies, ordered routing and admission guards, and code-derived retry safety replace scattered authorities. Generation 5 makes command identity mandatory.

04 / TRANSPORT
Finishing bytes is different from doing work.

Separate owners handle framing, validation, raw sockets, bounded lifecycle exchanges, accepted execution, and resumable result receipt. Appended records advance the resume position. Fetches keep transfer state; reattachments keep request identity but create fresh capture. Each has its own retry budget.

05 / DAEMON LIFE
Accepted work has a continuing identity.

The ledger deduplicates; one FIFO queue executes; delivery tracks the current stream; a generation manager fences old workers. Resources gate readiness and later turns. Activity uses explicit snapshots. Cleanup failure can be diagnostic while acknowledgement succeeds. Accepted failure never triggers local replay.

06 / CARRIED CHOICES
Preservation has a cost.

Idle time still starts at construction and resets on acceptance. Ledger eviction, startup silence, control-plane start readiness, endpoint relocation, new election, selection-aware byte retention, and readiness/completion idle changes are deferred. Tests lose or change some composed observations; the PR template also changes without a stated reason.

A SMALL MAP KEY

Symbol
A named code element, such as a function, class, or method.
Workspace
The code root chosen for the command. Nested repositories form separate boundaries.
Backend
The language-specific engine that answers code questions.
Snapshot / revision
A discovered set of files / the identity used to tell whether a file changed.
Turn
One refreshed opportunity to run a query. Prepared state may outlive it.
Ledger
The daemon's record of accepted requests and their completion states.
Spool
Stored output records waiting for delivery or acknowledgement; small output can stay in memory.
Generation
An identity for a worker lifetime, used to ignore reports from an older worker.
Cold / warm / fallback
Local execution / retained daemon execution / local execution after a recoverable daemon problem.
Facade / port / hook
A small public doorway / a limited capability interface / host-specific behavior supplied to a reusable base.
Admission / acceptance
Checks before taking work / the daemon's promise to own that request identity.
FIFO / backpressure
First accepted turn goes first / slow consumption makes the sender wait.

before the machinery.

01 / STATE
Retain preparation; renew meaning.

Source bytes, file indexes, project membership, and a session live longer than one query. Six independent semantic caches clear on a successful new turn or before release. Publication is per backend index or project graph; there is no whole-pipeline transaction. Selection refresh still evicts omitted source bytes.

02 / HOST
The host knows the product.

The CLI classifies syntax, resolves the workspace and state path, supplies an absolute executor module URL, and writes output. The daemon owns routing and captures warm output. The renderer also formats lifecycle reports. Build rules enforce the final package surface.

03 / POLICY & IDENTITY
One owner for each rule.

Immutable policy sections cross process and worker boundaries. Values stay fixed for users. One command vocabulary, distinct failure vocabularies, ordered routing and admission guards, and code-derived retry safety replace scattered authorities. Generation 5 makes command identity mandatory.

04 / TRANSPORT
Finishing bytes is different from doing work.

Separate owners handle framing, validation, raw sockets, bounded lifecycle exchanges, accepted execution, and resumable result receipt. Appended records advance the resume position. Fetches keep transfer state; reattachments keep request identity but create fresh capture. Each has its own retry budget.

05 / DAEMON LIFE
Accepted work has a continuing identity.

The ledger deduplicates; one FIFO queue executes; delivery tracks the current stream; a generation manager fences old workers. Resources gate readiness and later turns. Activity uses explicit snapshots. Cleanup failure can be diagnostic while acknowledgement succeeds. Accepted failure never triggers local replay.

06 / CARRIED CHOICES
Preservation has a cost.

Idle time still starts at construction and resets on acceptance. Ledger eviction, startup silence, control-plane start readiness, endpoint relocation, new election, selection-aware byte retention, and readiness/completion idle changes are deferred. Tests lose or change some composed observations; the PR template also changes without a stated reason.

Follow this boundary ↘

Accepted work stays accepted.

Codec, validator, socket directions, lifecycle, execution, receiver and capture split apart. FIFO accepts once. Duplicate requests attach. Fetch and reattachment have independent budgets; append precedes offset advancement.

Follow this boundary ↘

One daemon snapshot covers output, memory, retries, polling, diagnostics and deadlines. No user threshold knobs. Worker generations, sampled activity, clocks, registry identity and delivery barriers have explicit owners. Host-side policy is separate.

A package is not a process. The daemon package supplies client, process and worker code; its worker loads the host’s executor by file URL. Core is retained inside that executor and has no daemon or persistence port.

Preserve behavior is the stated aim.
Command bytes, exit codes, execution modes, and lifecycle outcomes should remain. The wire moves from generation 4 to 5 for explicit command identity. The game explains the chosen rules; it does not certify parity.
Test and workflow choices are part of the change.
Ten built CLI lifecycle scenarios are retired; raw log checks narrow to parsed events; a transfer test budget changes from 20 to 60 seconds; the PR template changes. Source-byte selection eviction, startup/acceptance-based idle timing, and other deferred behavior debts remain. All 20 observations and their rationale status ↓

ALL GAME RULES / VISIBLE BEFORE THE FIRST MOVE

Five open contracts
Read in order, or enter any station.
01
Rebuild the package map
Core gains source caching, revision/index transactions, project membership, turn-cache lifetime, and WorkspaceSession. TypeScript keeps tsconfig and semantic algorithms.
CLI keeps argv classification, workspace-root discovery, state-directory resolution, concrete executor composition, output selection and writes. Telemetry keeps usage logic.
Daemon gains routing, policy, registry, clocks, sockets, protocol, workers, execution, delivery, and spooling. Renderer gains lifecycle report formatting.
Core, daemon, and telemetry have no internal package dependencies. Backend → core; renderer → core and daemon; CLI → all five. Tests may additionally use testing utilities.
The daemon loads the host executor by an injected absolute file URL. That runtime handoff does not add a static daemon → CLI/core dependency. #148 stages copies; #149 switches the caller and removes them.

126.1
129.1
02
Separate three lifetimes
A revisioned index candidate is validated before toolchain commit and portable publication. Failure preserves that published index; ensureFiles commits one file at a time, retaining earlier progress.
ProjectGraph has its own validated publication transaction. This is not one atomic transaction across the whole backend or WorkspaceSession.
A failed refresh does not begin a semantic turn. A successful refresh begins the next turn and clears all six caches synchronously.
Within a turn, caches distinguish missing from cached undefined, preserve value/Promise identity and rejected Promises, and do not store a synchronous creator throw.
Release clears semantic caches before awaiting project cleanup, including when cleanup rejects. Session identity and reusable backend state survive; later releases can retry.
A selection opens fresh discovery without reconciling retained siblings. Source-byte caching still replaces its supplied snapshot and evicts omitted bytes; the prepared-file index has separate selection retention.
Play Keep the turn ↗
All decisions in this family ↓
123.2
124.2
124.3
03
Stop before the next side effect
Admission order is authentication → worker ready → resources not paused → queue accepting → duplicate compatibility. First failure ends evaluation; failed authentication disconnects without a rejection frame.
not-ready, resource-pressure, and draining allow local retry; incompatible does not. Retry safety is derived from the rejection code. A contradictory wire boolean is corruption.
Client routing reads a record, checks not starting, checks version, then probes responsiveness. Missing → cold/absent; starting → cold/starting; wrong version → fallback/incompatible; responsive compatible ready peer → warm.
Observation failures/unresponsive peers → cold/recovering; an exited peer permits conditional cleanup and fallback/dead. Daemon-disabled invocations bypass routing observation.
CLI classifies commandName once, separately from opaque argv. Duplicate compatibility includes that name. Generation 4 → 5 makes explicit command metadata mandatory; mixed versions use compatibility handling before execution.
Outer execution failures and worker failures remain separate vocabularies. Ordered classification preserves existing failure strings and client outcomes.
Play First gate wins ↗
All decisions in this family ↓
132.3
132.4
132.5
04
Keep one FIFO turn and one identity
The ledger owns immutable acceptance metadata. Matching duplicates attach to accepted work without a new execution, queue position, trace, clock read, or idle reset; conflicting duplicates are rejected earlier.
AcceptedExecutionSession composes ledger, queue, worker, delivery, resources, and process-lifecycle ports. Those dependencies keep their own state; FIFO work waits for the latest attached delivery, then boundary sampling gates the next turn.
WorkerGenerationManager shares one replacement operation: mark not ready, start the next generation, await termination of the old worker, then publish the new ready report. Old-generation exits cannot trigger recovery.
Initial readiness activation waits for warm-up sampling. After initial activation, replacement protocol-ready publication restores worker readiness. ResourceSupervisor separately completes replacement bookkeeping, reopens admission, and settles the boundary sample. Already-accepted B waits for that sample, not another admission pass.
Graceful close and forced termination have separate shared operations, so force can interrupt a blocked close. Resource policy owns replacement windows and the recovery circuit.
Activity is a pure snapshot projection with explicit clocks. It shows the worker’s in-progress generation, sampled spool usage, and the last fileCount in legacy pong even while readiness is false.
Play Hand off the worker ↗
All decisions in this family ↓
144.3

05
Move bytes without replaying work
The socket client owns pull-based reads and FIFO writes with backpressure; the server serializes each connection independently and shares an escalating shutdown operation. Codec/validator own framing, integrity, shape, and correlation.
Control connections decode JSON; execution-transfer connections also decode binary chunks. Lifecycle JSON and execution-control JSON have distinct capacities. Decoders are fresh on each connection.
One receiver retains manifest identity, digest progress, and a contiguous record offset across fetches. Offset advances only after awaited output append; fetch starts at the first record not durably captured.
A fetch continues the current capture. Reattaching identical accepted execution creates a fresh capture and receiver, disposes interrupted output, and keeps the same daemon request identity without local replay.
Default budgets are one fetch resume per execution attempt and one accepted-execution reattachment. A reattached attempt gets its own fetch allowance. Exhausted fetches preserve accepted-corruption failure; acceptance has no completion deadline.
Manifest identity, record count, byte total and digest must match before success. Client acknowledgement uses the lifecycle client; failure disposes output. Successful finish transfers capture ownership to the caller, who eventually disposes it.
Server acknowledgement attempts physical spool cleanup before logical ledger acknowledgement; cleanup failure is diagnostic and does not withhold protocol success. Acknowledged ledger identity still remains; eviction is deferred.

CLI composes one immutable, versioned DaemonPolicy from system memory; process and worker boundaries carry its complete values. Consumers require slices. There is no user tuning surface. These are the tip’s recorded values and reasons, not measurements made by this game.

HEALTHY STARTUP
None

Progressing warm-up has no project-size deadline.

STARTUP SILENCE
None

Silence handling is deferred to the daemon follow-up contract.

POST-ACCEPT COMPLETION
None

Accepted work is not replayed or failed because it runs long.

WORKER OUTPUT ACKNOWLEDGEMENT
None

Backpressure waits for durable consumption without a timer.

UNACKNOWLEDGED RESULT
None

Retention eviction is deferred to the daemon follow-up contract.

About experiment 24 ↗
SYMNAV #127
THE COMPLETE OVERVIEW
What can a cache remember?

TypeScript keeps the query logic. Core takes ownership of forgetting. Six caches keep their identities, and the backend now waits for project cleanup.

THE SHAPE OF A TURN
Ask. Ask again.
Reuse the same cached entry.
→
Cross a boundary.
Next successful refresh, or release.
→
Ask afresh.
The handles are still usable.
Simplified: the six marks stand for six caches. Clearing drops stored entries; it does not revoke values or cancel promises held elsewhere.

These seven answers are the whole change. Every question below adds detail to them.

Stated = a reason is recorded in the PR or spec. Unexplained = the choice is visible, but its reason was not found.

01 · OWNERSHIP
Who owns forgetting?
TypeScript queries
→
core scope
→
6 maps

Manual map clearing moves into TurnScopedCacheScope in core: cache lifetime is language-independent. Each query service creates its own scope and six typed handles. Algorithms, keys, and projections stay in TypeScript; the import still points from TypeScript to core.

The service contains a scope. The spec describes a shared base that a backend extends; the reason for choosing composition here is unrecorded.

D1 · owner stated
D2 · composition unexplained
02 · REUSE
What stays shared?
5 symbol → promises
1 position → locations

Six separate key/value spaces remain separate. The handle returns the exact stored value, including undefined and empty arrays. Presence uses Map.has, because undefined can be a cached value.

Callers and references share reference discovery. Public reference results and syntax-node arrays are projected again on access; the underlying cached locations are reused.

D3 · isolation stated
D4 · identity & presence stated
03 · TURN
When does a turn end?
refresh succeeds
→
clear every cache

The next turn begins only after the source, applicable project, and workspace-state refresh steps succeed—even with unchanged files. A failed refresh keeps the current cache entries. That ordering is preserved from the base; it is not a promise to roll back all refresh side effects.

Both lifecycle calls synchronously empty values. Handles survive and can refill; there is no phase guard, cancellation, timer, per-key invalidation, or handle-disposal API.

D5 · success boundary stated
D9 · minimal lifecycle unexplained
04 · RELEASE
When is release actually finished?
clear now
→
await projects
→
settle backend

Before, project cleanup was started without awaiting it. Now the service and backend await it. Old entries disappear before cleanup can stay pending or reject; the backend's release promise waits and propagates the error.

Clearing does not lock out queries. The spec promises unchanged timing and failure paths; the PR states the new release barrier, but records no reconciliation with that broader parity promise.

D6 · release order stated
Parity reconciliation unexplained
05 · FAILURE
Does a failed answer get reused?
rejected promise: kept
sync throw: retry

The existing distinction survives. A returned promise is stored as-is, including rejection; a factory that throws before returning stores nothing and runs again on a later lookup.

Clearing does not cancel an old promise. That promise may still settle, but settlement alone cannot overwrite a new turn's entry: the cache installs no settlement callback.

D7 · failure & identity preservation stated
06 · PUBLIC SURFACE
What do callers have to change?
+ core export
snapshot → files
void → Promise

Core exports the scope and the getOrCreate-only handle interface. The service's beginTurn now takes a readonly file list instead of a workspace snapshot; no reason for that narrowing is recorded.

The service's release return type becomes Promise<void>. The backend already returned a promise; its signature stays, its awaited boundary expands.

D1/D6 · export & await stated
D8/D9 · narrowing & API limits unexplained
07 · EVIDENCE
What do the tests tell us?

Where the picture breaks: clearing removes cache entries, not work already running. A caller can still hold an old promise. The counter is not locked during release, so a later query can refill a drawer.

01 / THE WHOLE CHANGE
ALL DECISIONS BEFORE THE DETAIL
Eight things to carry away.

Stated = a reason exists in the supplied PR or plan. Unexplained = the choice is present, but no reason was found in the inspected inputs.

1
Move the clearing mechanism into core.
STATED

The language-neutral scope is reusable. Each TypeScript service still constructs and owns its own scope; algorithms, source cache and project graph stay in their existing roles.

Package & instance boundaries ↘
2
Keep six independent address spaces.
STATED

One scope, six typed handles, one map per handle. Existing keys and value types stay separate; a shared key never makes two query kinds share an entry.

Open all six drawers ↘
3
Keep the exact entries and failure behavior.
STATED

Reuse values and promises, including empties; the new generic primitive also accepts undefined. Rejected promises stay cached; synchronous factory throws are retried. Reference and position locations are still rehydrated on access.

Tickets, failures & projections ↘
4
Finish refresh before starting a turn.
STATED

Successful refresh clears all six, even for unchanged files. A failed refresh never reaches that clearing step, preserving the current semantic-cache turn. This ordering already existed.

Replay success or failure ↘
5
Clear first; await project release next.
STATED

Clearing stays synchronous. The service now returns a promise and the backend awaits it, so a pending or rejected graph release reaches the caller. The graph’s existing release order is unchanged.

Replay the changed barrier ↘
6
Clearing is reusable, not terminal.
UNEXPLAINED

No turn token, cancellation, closed flag or query lock. Both signals empty the same registered handles; repeated clearing is allowed. Old promises can settle without replacing new entries, and queries can refill during release.

The analogy’s limits ↘
7
Expose a small cache API; pass fewer inputs.
UNEXPLAINED

Core exports the scope and lookup-only handle type. Handles expose no clearing operation. The service’s beginTurn takes a file list instead of a full snapshot; this is documented without a separate rationale.

Exact public signatures ↘
8
Characterize, then extract.
STATED

Four new core tests and six new service tests pin the preservation contract. Five previous service tests remain with their assertions intact. The new pending/rejected-release case uses a graph test double; the real fixture also remains.

Test scope & source receipts ↘

WHAT OCCUPIES A CACHE ENTRY
Factory behavior	What the handle retains	Next lookup for that key
Returns an object or array	The same object, including an empty array	Same identity; factory is skipped
Returns undefined	A present entry whose value is undefined	Same value; Map.has prevents a repeat call
Returns a promise that rejects	That exact promise, still cached after rejection	Same rejection; no automatic retry

The undefined row describes the new generic core contract. The six TypeScript caches store promises or arrays; this PR does not turn a previously uncached TypeScript undefined result into a hit.

A stored location is not a stored live node.

Position definitions keep location records, including an empty list, then find nodes again for every access. Reference lookups similarly share location work while building reference projections per call.

The inherited graph releases configured projects in order, awaiting returned promises, then the inferred project. This PR connects that completion to the backend; the concrete TypeScript project cleanup itself is synchronous.

↑ Back to the whole change
An empty drawer is not a closed counter.
No cancellation

Clearing drops the map’s reference. An old promise can still settle for its existing caller. The cache installs no settlement callback, so that settlement cannot insert an old result over a new entry.

B

STATED a source supplies a reason
UNEXPLAINED no specific reason found in the inspected inputs
01
Cut coordination, keep the owners
Two coordinators; the same process and package.
STATED

#146 extracts delivery and trace coordination. #147 extracts acceptance and FIFO execution. Both still live in apps/cli/src/daemon; CLI and protocol surfaces stay put.

Reason: Attachment, transfer, acknowledgement and trace lifecycles form one boundary; existing mechanisms retain their owners.

Share authoritative owners through selected ports.
STATED

The ledger owns request state; the spool store owns bytes; the queue owns FIFO order. Only some dependencies have small interfaces; several still use concrete class types.

Reason: The author explicitly keeps each mechanism authoritative instead of moving its state into either session.

Delivery lands first; the reason for two PRs is unstated.
UNEXPLAINED

#147 consumes the writer, trace and barrier surface introduced by #146. The order is documented; no comparison with a combined or reversed split was found.

Missing reason: The bodies say “delivery before accepted execution.” They do not explain why this exact review boundary was chosen.

02
One acceptance, many connections
Acceptance metadata moves from a shell map to the ledger.
STATED

acceptedAt and the original queuePosition survive queued, running, terminal and acknowledged states. Navigation activity is sampled separately.

Reason: Every state shares one original acceptance identity; a parallel process map duplicated that ownership.

A matching duplicate attaches; it does not run again.
STATED

The shell passes the same acceptance envelope to delivery. Execution adds no trace, queue turn, clock read or lifetime reset for an existing matching request.

Reason: Request identity stays idempotent for the lifetime of this daemon.

The shell authenticates; the “Authenticated” aliases add no check.
UNEXPLAINED

Both sessions receive requests already checked by the shell. Their new Authenticated… types are aliases of the original request types, without a type-level proof.

Missing reason: No reason was found for choosing aliases over another way to express the caller’s authentication responsibility.

03
Lend handles across the cut
Execution borrows a writer; delivery wraps the spool timing.
STATED

The writer crosses to the worker for ordered byte appends, then execution finishes or disposes it. The spool store remains the owner of completion bytes.

Reason: The author keeps completion bytes in their existing owner and coordinates their lifecycle through delivery.

Delivery owns retention; execution gets a fenced trace handle.
STATED

Late events stop when the trace expires or is evicted. Only disconnected traces are bounded; attachments are counted, and terminal delivery is recorded once in the ledger.

Reason: Evicted or expired traces must ignore late diagnostics even when execution still holds a handle.

04
Keep the waits inside the turn
The current delivery promise holds the FIFO turn.
STATED

Execution captures the latest tracked stream’s promise after ledger publication. It waits for that stream, not all attachments or a normal ACK; later fetches do not retarget the wait. A caught send failure also settles it.

Reason: Queue completion must wait for the current stream without creating another request registry.

A resource sample gates the next turn after success or failure.
STATED

Twelve choices, with their reasons
Why this order ↗

“Stated” means a source gives a reason. “Unexplained” means no reason was found in the bounded PR/commit/plan corpus; the choice may still be explicitly declared. The PR promises preservation, while release completion and failure visibility change. That distinction remains visible below.

01 / The moved boundaries
D01
REASON: STATED
Give six caches one clearing owner

Core owns clearing for all six handles; TypeScript keeps the query algorithms. Five handles use symbol identities, one uses file positions. Their key and value spaces stay separate.

Independent query key and value spaces are the stated reason for six handles.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
D12
REASON: UNEXPLAINED
Carry project completion and failure back to the backend

Backend release now waits for the graph's completion and propagates its rejection, including failure that stops later project releases. This is an observable contract change alongside the ownership move. The PR declares the barrier, but the broad plan promises unchanged failure behavior; no separate rationale reconciles that change. The generic graph already returns a promise even though concrete TypeScript cleanup is synchronous.

The awaited barrier is explicit, but no separate reason reconciles changed failure/completion visibility with the plan's preservation promise. The stated clearing-order reason belongs to D02.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
D02
REASON: STATED
Empty entries before project release

Old cache entries disappear synchronously when release starts, even while project release is pending or rejects. The ordering is preserved; the clearing owner changes.

The PR says released semantics must be unavailable while release is pending or rejecting.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
D03
REASON: STATED
Advance the cache turn only after refresh succeeds

Successful refresh clears the previous turn, even for unchanged files. Failed refresh never reaches beginTurn, so it keeps the prior cache entries and query-file list. This is a cache guarantee, not a claim that every refresh side effect is rolled back.

The PR says failed refresh must preserve the current successful turn.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
02 / Declared surfaces, missing reasons
D04
REASON: UNEXPLAINED
Use a scope object at the package seam

The service composes a core scope. The plan describes shared backend bases and inheritance; the PR shows this composed form, without giving a reason for that form. The existing TypeScript → core dependency direction is retained.

The PR describes composition but gives no reason for choosing it over the plan's base/extends wording.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
D05
REASON: UNEXPLAINED
Expose reusable handles and whole-scope clearing

The public handle offers getOrCreate; scope methods clear every registered handle synchronously. Handles remain usable before beginTurn, after repeated release, and during pending project release. There is no turn gate, per-key invalidation, or handle-unregister operation; the service creates its six handles once.

The public surface is stated; no reason is given for this minimal, reusable lifecycle contract.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
D06
REASON: UNEXPLAINED
Pass a file list across the exported service API

The already-exported semantic service now takes a file list instead of a whole snapshot. The backend supplies snapshot.files. Direct callers of that public method must change their argument shape; the PR records the signature change without explaining why.

No reason for the narrower argument is stated in the PR, commits, or relevant plan passages.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
03 / Contracts kept and made generic
D08
REASON: STATED
Return the exact factory value between clears

Between clears, a repeated key on one handle returns the same value or promise object. Clearing forgets entries without cancelling returned work. An old promise may settle later but cannot overwrite a new-turn entry. Promise identity applies at the cached service/handle boundary, not every async wrapper.

The PR's compatibility intent explicitly preserves promise/value identities; it gives no separate optimization claim.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
D09
REASON: STATED
Keep async failures cached; retry synchronous throws

A factory that returns a promise stores it, including later rejection, until the next clear. A factory that throws synchronously stores nothing, so the next access retries. TypeScript definitions/callees take the async path; reference discovery can take the synchronous path.

The stated reason is compatibility with existing failure behavior; no independent defense of the asymmetry is supplied.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
D07
REASON: STATED
Treat undefined as a cached value

A present key is a hit even when its value is undefined. Existing TypeScript caches hold arrays or promises; the generic core contract also supports undefined without rerunning the factory.

The PR explicitly names undefined as a valid cached value.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
D10
REASON: STATED
Keep TypeScript projections and query work in place

Query keys and bodies stay in TypeScript. Observers run on cache misses; callers and references share cached reference locations. Position caches keep locations (including empty results), while each access rebuilds a node array. Reference results are also projected per access; the refactor does not turn all outputs into shared objects.

The PR explicitly preserves all six algorithms, key spaces, and value identities.

Mechanism & evidence ↗
D11
REASON: STATED
Add contract tests while retaining prior assertions

Ten new tests cover identities/isolation, empty-position projection, rejection versus throw, successful-turn preservation, immediate clearing plus awaited release, repeated release, and late promise settlement. The five existing tests remain; none is weakened or deleted. The pending/rejecting release case uses a controlled graph double. This artifact inspects tests; it does not report a test run.

The PR names characterization and identity/error/clearing contracts, alongside its compatibility intent.

6 changed files
4th layer in a 26-PR stack

Read the map and decisions. Stop here, or follow any box.

construct / beginTurn / release

Simplified code ownership: only the relevant classes are shown. The scope is a TypeScript-held object implemented in core; all of these calls remain in one process. Click a box to follow it.

New lifetime implementation / handle boundary
Manual clearing moves out of TypeScript

A turn is a cache lifetime. It starts after a successful backend refresh. Release clears entries immediately, but does not cancel returned promises or block new queries. The new wait belongs to the TypeScript release chain.

THE DECISIONS / COMPLETE AT THIS LEVEL

What a reader needs to weigh

Reasons come from the PR and spec. Two API choices have no located rationale. The release barrier also meets a stricter parity promise in the stack spec.

01
REASON STATED
Put cache lifetime in core

Export TurnScopedCacheScope and its typed handle from core. TypeScript still chooses when to begin a turn and release; core clears the entries.

The architecture spec assigns shared cache lifecycle to core and semantic query bodies to the language backend.

See how it works ↗
Reason source ↗
02
REASON STATED
Keep six independent caches

One scope owns six separate typed handles: definitions, references, call targets, callers, callees, and position definitions. Each keeps its own Map.

The PR explicitly chooses isolated handles over a shared map because the queries have independent key and value spaces.

See how it works ↗
Reason source ↗
03
REASON STATED
Return the exact cached value

Keep the existing identity and file-position keys. Cache values and promises without wrapping them. A stored undefined or empty array is still a hit; use Map.has.

The PR promises preserved keys and identities and names undefined as the reason for checking membership before reading.

See how it works ↗
Reason source ↗
04
REASON STATED
Keep two different failure paths

A returned promise stays cached even after rejection. A factory that throws before returning stores nothing, so the next lookup retries it.

The PR's context commits to preserving existing failure behavior. New tests characterize asynchronous query failures and synchronous reference failures.

See how it works ↗
Reason source ↗
05
REASON STATED
Start a turn after refresh succeeds

Keep the existing order: refresh source/project/workspace state, then clear all six caches. A failed refresh does not begin a new semantic-cache turn.

The PR says a failed refresh must preserve the current successful turn. This is an existing boundary being retained.

See how it works ↗
Reason source ↗
06
REASON STATED
Clear immediately; make release wait

Keep synchronous clearing before project release. Now the service and backend await project release, so its pending state and rejection reach the caller. The stack spec also asks for unchanged failure paths.

The PR says released semantics must be unavailable while release is pending or rejecting. It requests the awaited barrier; reconciliation with the stack's parity wording is unexplained.

See how it works ↗
Reason source ↗
07
REASON STATED
Keep TypeScript's query work

Keep algorithms and miss observers in TypeScript. Cache reference/position locations, then rebuild reference projections and node arrays on access; those outward arrays and wrapper promises need not share cache identity.

The PR says this layer moves only cache lifetime while preserving all six algorithms. The spec reserves semantic query bodies for TypeScript.

See how it works ↗
Reason source ↗
08
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Accept files instead of a snapshot

Change the exported service's beginTurn input from WorkspaceSnapshot to readonly WorkspaceFile[]. The backend now passes snapshot.files; the service retains that file list.

The PR lists the signature change, but gives no reason for narrowing this public input. No reason found in its commits or the supplied specs.

See how it works ↗
09
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Compose a scope that can be reused

The service constructs a scope rather than extending a base. Handles expose getOrCreate only. Clearing retains handles and file inputs, cancels no promise, and permits new cache entries even while project release is pending.

No rationale found for composition over a base or for a reusable, non-revoking API. The spec describes shared bases; the code keeps a registry of handles with no disposal operation.

See how it works ↗
10
REASON STATED
Add tests around preserved contracts

Add six TypeScript cases and four core cases for identities, empty results/rehydration, failures, clearing, failed refresh, awaited release, and old-promise settlement. Keep all five previous TypeScript tests and their assertions.

The commits explicitly characterize identities and specify lifecycle/release. This supports the PR's preservation intent. These are source assertions, not a report of tests run here.

See how it works ↗
Reason source ↗

That is the overview. The next layers unpack these same ten choices and show their source.

Continue through the mechanisms ↗

02 / MECHANISM

Follow one choice all the way down.

Every section returns to its decision. The next-section links also form a continuous reading path.

DECISION 01 / MECHANISM

Put cache lifetime in core
← Return to decision 01

The package containing the lifetime implementation changes. The caller that decides when to clear stays in TypeScript. Core exports both the scope class and the handle type; the concrete handle class is private.

Schematic dependency map; abbreviated declarations. The public handle surface and choice of composition are also visible in decision 09.

Follow the reusable scope ↗
Read the source evidence ↗
Next: Keep six independent caches ↗

DECISION 02 / MECHANISM

Keep six independent caches
← Return to decision 02

The service creates each handle once as an instance field. A handle gets its own Map, so the same key can select different values in different query families.

symbol key → promise of definitions
referencesByIdentity
symbol key → promise of reference locations
callTargetsByIdentity
symbol key → promise of resolution
callersByIdentity
symbol key → promise of caller edges
calleesByIdentity
symbol key → promise of callee edges
definitionsByPosition
file:start → semantic location array

Outer boundary: one scope. Inner boxes: independent Maps behind typed handles.

Next: Return the exact cached value ↗

DECISION 03 / MECHANISM

Return the exact cached value
← Return to decision 03
Lookup	Stored entry	Factory call	Returned value
First lookup of k	Absent	Runs once	The exact result V is stored and returned
Repeat lookup of k	V exists	Skipped	The same V, including an empty array
Repeat lookup of k	undefined exists	Skipped	undefined; presence is checked with Map.has
Same key, another handle	Independent Map	Runs in that handle	That handle's own V

Five caches keep formatSymbolIdentity(identity) keys. The position cache keeps relativePath:node.getStart(). The handle returns a promise as an ordinary value; it adds no async wrapper. Outward projections are covered in decision 07.

Keep two different failure paths
← Return to decision 04

The promise is stored immediately.
↓
Promise later rejects
The cached object remains the same.
↓

← Return to decision 06

Backend calls service
The backend method already returns Promise<void>.

Service clears all six Maps
Synchronous, before project release.

Simplified sequence with an asynchronous project release. Core cache clearing itself has no await.

Two stated intentions meet here. The PR requests an awaited release barrier. The architecture spec requests unchanged failure paths. The changed promise chain exposes a project-release rejection to the backend caller. Neither document explains how these two intentions are reconciled.

Clearing removes cached entries, not every reference ever returned. Queries can repopulate caches while release is pending; the added test deliberately does so. See decision 09 for that lifetime limit.

What clearing does to existing handles ↗

Next: Keep TypeScript's query work ↗

DECISION 07 / MECHANISM

Keep TypeScript's query work
← Return to decision 07
Cache / public operation	What is shared	What is produced on access
findDefinitions / findCallTarget / findCallers / findCallees	Each service method's own cached promise	The same promise within that handle and turn
findReferences	Internal referenceLocations promise, also used by callers	A reference projection array after awaiting locations
definitionNodesOf	Semantic location array, including an empty one	A new array of rehydrated nodes; node objects can be identical

Miss observers remain inside factories, so a cache hit skips the observer and underlying search. TypeScript still finds definitions, discovers references, builds caller/callee edges, classifies references, and locates syntax nodes. Core stores values without knowing these algorithms.

Identity is a cache-level contract, not a claim that every backend method or outward projection returns the same Promise object.

DECISION 08 / MECHANISM

← Return to decision 08

After · file list

The only changed production call passes request.snapshot.files. Both versions retain the file list by reference. The service is exported by the TypeScript package; the input type change is therefore part of its public surface.

Reason unexplained. The PR names the new signature. It does not say why the snapshot parameter was narrowed as part of moving cache lifetime.

Read the source evidence ↗
Next: Compose a scope that can be reused ↗

DECISION 09 / MECHANISM

Compose a scope that can be reused
← Return to decision 09
Handle lifetime
Service constructs a scope
One registry stores all created handles.
↓
beginTurn or release clears entries
Each registered Map is cleared; the registry remains.
↓
The same handle is called again
It can store a new entry immediately.
Returned promise lifetime
An old promise P was returned
The caller already holds P.
↓
A clear happens; new promise Q is cached
Clearing has no cancellation or settlement hook.
↓
P settles later
P still settles; the cache still contains Q.

Illustrative ordering, not cancellation or a concurrency protocol. The scope has no active-turn flag, revocation, disposal, or per-entry eviction API.

The typed consumer sees only getOrCreate. The scope alone exposes beginTurn and releaseTransientResources, both synchronous. Neither operation resets the service’s files. Composition is concrete in new TurnScopedCacheScope(); the architecture spec’s wording describes shared bases.

Reason unexplained. The source and tests show these choices, but the searched PR, commit bodies, and specs do not explain choosing this composed, reusable API over an inherited or revocable one.

ONE WAY IN

Six trays.
One closing routine.

Picture a TypeScript workbench with six trays of reusable answers. The specialist still does the work. A reusable organizer now owns the trays’ clearing routine. Wiping the trays and finishing the workshop’s shutdown are separate moments.

The specialist keeps the tools
Six trays keep different kinds of answers apart.
The organizer empties the trays
Previously stored answers stop being available immediately.
The supervisor waits for shutdown
Only then does the closing call finish or report failure.

Core supplies the organizer; each TypeScript query service owns one. The backend waits for project cleanup. A fresh work session starts only after refresh succeeds.

Metaphor: trays are caches, not work queues. Emptying them neither cancels work nor closes access to a cleared tray afterward.

01 / THE WHOLE CHANGE

Six stores stay separate.
Their lifetime gets one owner.

TypeScript still computes the answers. Core supplies the cache mechanism. The backend now waits for project release.

02 / OWNERSHIP · D1–D2

The service chooses the stores.
The scope clears them together.
↑ Back to D1
One query service
Constructs one scope.

→

STATED · D1–D2

The spec places shareable lifecycle behavior in core and toolchain-specific query bodies in TypeScript. The PR chooses six handles over one shared map because the existing key and value spaces are independent.

Static boundary
TypeScript imports TurnScopedCacheScope from core. Core’s new cache file has no imports and knows nothing about TypeScript nodes or symbols.

Open the record
↗
03
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Retire the temporary policy-testing export and its checks

Remove @symnav/daemon/policy-testing. Put override factories in CLI/package test helpers; update imports and lock exact root + process-entry + worker-entry exports. Delete the special lint restriction, its two lint tests, and the temporary-subpath export/declaration tests.

WHY RECORDED

No separate rationale for this export retirement and the associated test deletions was found in the PR body, commit bodies, or supplied plans.

Open the record
↗
02
The client owns the consequences of a route

Keep the order, the independent warm-up, the replay boundary, and the output owner together.

04
REASON STATED
Keep the public façade free of Node ambient types

Expose DaemonClient.execute/control and portable contracts. Dynamically import its private Node runtime through a string-typed module URL; loading begins in the constructor, and each method awaits the same runtime promise. This is a declaration boundary, not browser execution support.

WHY RECORDED

Host declarations must not acquire Node ambient dependencies.

Open the record
↗
05
REASON STATED
The first routing decision stops later observation

Disabled execution bypasses registry routing. Otherwise evaluate record present → not starting → version compatible → responsive, in that order. Read/observe lazily and memoize each operation. Missing, starting, recovering, dead, incompatible, and warm routes keep their distinct effects; only confirmed exit asks routing to remove the record.

WHY RECORDED

The first routing decision must prevent every later side effect.

Open the record
↗
06
REASON STATED
Answer locally without waiting for warm-up

Cold/fallback attempts create a fresh host executor. Absent records and fallback routes trigger startup independently; starting/recovering routes do not. Swallow background trigger failures, preserve the chosen route, forward argv/cwd/telemetry, and give local executors a no-op resource sampler.

WHY RECORDED

Ordinary commands must answer locally while a daemon warms; a daemon becoming ready must not cancel or duplicate local work.

Open the record
↗
07
REASON STATED
Replay warm work only when transport says it is safe

Use the existing DaemonTransportError.retrySafe authority for one local fallback. Uncertain submission, accepted-work failure, non-retry-safe rejection, and malformed/failed completion stay warm and return a controlled failure; they do not replay locally or invalidate ownership through this client path.

WHY RECORDED

Timeout or disconnect is not evidence that a healthy daemon or accepted work can be discarded.

Open the record
↗
08
REASON STATED
Own warm output capture and controlled failure bytes

Create fresh result captures in the OS temporary directory from output policy; the public host supplies no storage/output factory. Package-private transport accepts an internal capture factory. Map resource/response/other failures to three stderr messages with exit code 1; malformed exit codes or missing output become controlled warm failures, disposing available malformed output.

WHY RECORDED

Warm transfer cleanup and replay safety belong to the daemon client.

Open the record
↗
09
REASON STATED
The host supplies product knowledge, including the readiness probe

Options require state directory, product version, enabled flag, executor factory/module URL, and readiness probe; policy is optional. Execute receives workspace root, command name, argv, cwd, and telemetry. Forward the host's readiness command/argv through startup with telemetry off and legacy cold mode; the internal coordinator retains a --version default.

WHY RECORDED

The daemon must run commands without knowing what they are; CLI syntax stays in the host.

Open the record
↗
10
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Keep lifecycle composition inside the client

Reuse composed controllers and a startup coordinator. Give status its own response timeout/transport, keep start and stop on the routing transport, and let mechanism errors reject for a host wrapper. Typed overloads return one action's report. Disabled blocks start, while status and stop remain callable.

WHY RECORDED

The host-facing control boundary is specified; no separate reason was found for this exact controller/timeout composition or the disabled-control asymmetry.

Open the record
↗
03
Identity and time have named owners

The extraction also narrowed construction, centralized startup equality, and preserved the old lifetime behavior.

11
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Validate process coordinates before composing its internals

Rename WorkspaceDaemon to DaemonProcessCoordinator. Replace loose identity fields with supplied coordinates validated against workspace root/keys/endpoint at constructor entry; adopt that endpoint. Require a DaemonClock, rename transport to a serving-only server, narrow filesystem injection to workspaceExists, and characterize cyclic callbacks as bound but not invoked during construction.

WHY RECORDED

The architecture requests a process coordinator; the commits specify these construction choices without recording why this exact contract was chosen.

Open the record
↗
12
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Preserve the request-specific authentication order

Add characterization around the existing process request dispatcher: identify/terminate/kill use their credential paths before the general protocol/instance gate; ping uses that gate; execute checks its token before admission observations; execution-status/result-fetch/result-ack validate tokens before ledger or delivery access. The remaining stop path drains accepted work and waits for acknowledgements.

WHY RECORDED

The PR adds order-sensitive tests and adopts the new coordinate fields; no rationale for the inherited request-by-request authentication asymmetry was found.

Open the record
↗
13
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Ask the registry which startup owner still matches

Centralize startup-owner equality in the registry and replace caller comparisons with named operations. Match identity+instance always, credentials/kind/PID only when required, and full acquiredAt/heartbeatAt/revision snapshots for owner-sensitive mutations. Preserve guarded writes, ownership rereads, launcher handoff, and cleanup against changed owners.

WHY RECORDED

A single lock-ownership authority is requested in the architecture spec. No separate rationale for the narrow-versus-full comparison choices was found.

Open the record
↗
14
REASON STATED
Daemon time comes through DaemonClock

Remove the lifetime's telemetry Clock dependency and scattered time callbacks. Use wallNowMs for lifetime, ledger timestamps, registry leases, controller/termination deadlines, and replacement windows; use monotonicNowMs for queue/activity and worker durations. The process injects one clock into its composed owners; NodeDaemonClock owns the two real sources.

WHY RECORDED

The architecture gives the daemon its own wall and monotonic clock instead of using telemetry as shared utilities.

Open the record
↗
15
REASON STATED
Do not remember the deferred idle changes as shipped

Keep the constructor-started, navigation-acceptance-reset idle deadline. Completion only marks the queue idle; if the deadline has passed, idle shutdown can begin then. Record readiness-armed and completion-based idle intervals as two future behavior changes, leaving the interval itself unchanged.

WHY RECORDED

Readiness- and completion-based lifetime changes are explicitly deferred behavior.

Open the record
↗
04
The evidence moved, and some of it changed

37 mechanism test files moved. The deletions, narrower checks, platform branch, and test configuration are decisions too.

16
REASON STATED
Move mechanism tests to their package owner

Move 37 app-local mechanism test files into daemon source directories, with package-local helpers and generic executor fixtures. Keep CLI integration/e2e ownership in the app; the changed e2e expectations are unchanged apart from helper imports/names. Add façade, routing, contract, boundary, registry, construction, and built-entry characterization.

WHY RECORDED

The extraction spec directs tests that reach into daemon internals to use the public surface or move into the package.

Open the record
↗
17
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Delete the mocked CLI entry tests; add package entry evidence

Delete daemon-entry.test.ts and its two app-local cases: configuration/logger/termination-observer wiring and source independence. Add package production/entry boundary checks and real built worker, launcher, and process-entry tests for configuration, one initialization, missing modules/exports, and ownership cleanup. They exercise different boundaries.

WHY RECORDED

The commits name the retirement and the built-entry proofs, but no reason is recorded for discarding those exact mock-level observations or treating the replacement evidence as sufficient.

Open the record
↗
18
REASON UNEXPLAINED
The moved worker test no longer exercises the same CLI integration

Replace the injected CLI readiness scenario with a generic executor; remove its discovery/indexing/total duration expectations. Delete the worker-level CLI version-mismatch initialization-failure test; restore version rejection as a direct CLI executor-factory test. Generic module failures remain tested, but the old combined CLI-worker path is no longer that test.

WHY RECORDED

Package independence is a stated extraction constraint. No reason was found for the loss of the duration assertions or for replacing that worker-level rejection observation with a factory-level one.

Open the record
↗
19
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Windows termination has a different cleanup witness

The new built-process test branches on win32: after termination it expects the ready record to remain and no process-termination diagnostic, then the test harness removes the exited process record. Other platforms expect self-cleanup and that diagnostic. Both branches finally assert no record or owner.

WHY RECORDED

The final commit specifies the platform branch. It provides no body explaining the OS-level reason or why this is the chosen observation.

Open the record
↗
20
REASON UNEXPLAINED
Make daemon test files run serially and add tsx

Add a daemon-specific Vitest configuration with fileParallelism: false, and add tsx ^4.21.0 as a daemon dev dependency with a lockfile update. This changes the test execution setup alongside the extraction.

WHY RECORDED

No reason for disabling test-file parallelism or for the exact new dev-dependency choice was found in the PR body, commit bodies, or supplied plans.

STATED
Move the lifetime owner

Core exports the generic scope and cache interface. TypeScript keeps semantic algorithms, key construction and project resources; its service calls into core.

Plan: language-independent retention belongs in core.

02
STATED
Share expiry, isolate stores

One scope owns six typed stores: five promise caches by symbol identity and one location cache by file position. Callers reuse reference discovery; call-target resolution reuses definitions.

PR: the existing key and value spaces are independent.

STATED

UNEXPLAINED
Reuse locations; project again

Locations cache; reference promises/results and position node arrays are fresh on access. Position nodes are looked up again and can be the same node. This existing behavior stays. Backend async wrappers are a separate boundary.

Preservation is requested; the specific reason for reprojecting locations is not given.

Contributor guide calls for informative tests before implementation.

↗

Reconcile the release promise

The PR introduces awaited release; the larger spec promises unchanged lifecycle outcomes. A deferred/rejecting injected graph changes completion/error behavior; concrete TypeScript cleanup is synchronous here. No reconciliation is recorded.

The local ordering rationale is stated. Its fit with global parity is not.

EXPERIMENT 37 / PR #127 / LAYER 4 OF 26
Experiment notes ↗

SCOPE SEMANTIC CACHES TO ONE TURN

Same query work.
A different clearing hand.

LOSSY INTUITION
Six drawers keep their contents separate. A shared caretaker now empties them. The drawers are caches, not processes.

Core takes cache lifetime; TypeScript keeps the algorithms. Successful refresh still resets the turn. Release clears first, and now waits for project release to finish or reject.

3 reasons not found
THE PACKAGE SEAM

AFTER

algorithms · holds scope instance
create / use

one synchronous clearing loop
RELEASE COMPLETION NOW CROSSES THIS WHOLE CHAIN
TypeScriptBackend

Boxes show source ownership. The TypeScript service holds the runtime scope instance. No process moves.
07

Keep this boundary in view. The PR says failure behavior is preserved and also introduces an awaited release barrier. The source shows changed completion timing and rejection propagation. A reason reconciling these claims was not found.

Locate this decision →

A REVIEW WITH TWO INDEPENDENT DIRECTIONS

Keep a fact. Change its depth.
Keep a depth. Change the fact.

Read the twelve threads down the left for the complete change. Select any crossing to inspect it. The right-hand pane holds your place.

On a crossing: ↑↓ change decision · ←→ change depth · Esc return to Shape.

Unroll the full review ↓
THE COMPLETE SURFACE
Reasons are part of the surface.
Shape
Choice
Mechanism
Evidence
01
Move lifetime across the package seam

Core gains the generic cache lifetime owner. The TypeScript query service holds its instance and keeps the semantic algorithms. The existing TypeScript → core dependency direction stays the same.

STATEDThe architecture spec assigns language-independent retention to core; the PR explicitly moves only cache lifetime.

1
2
3
4
02
Keep six independent compartments

Five handles keep promises under formatted symbol identities; a sixth keeps location arrays under file:position keys. Keys, value types, and exact cached identities stay separate. Callers and references still share reference-location work.

STATEDThe PR chooses six handles over a shared map because the queries have independent key and value spaces.

1
2
3
4
03
An undefined value still occupies a key

The generic handle tests membership with Map.has, then returns Map.get. A stored undefined is a hit. The factory runs only when the key is absent; the TypeScript cache value types themselves are unchanged.

STATEDThe PR says undefined is a valid cached value, so truthiness cannot decide whether a key exists.

1
2
3
4
04
A rejected promise sticks; a thrown factory retries

The handle stores returned promises without wrapping or awaiting them, including later rejection. A synchronous throw happens before storage and retries next time. Query observers remain inside cache-fill factories and run on attempted fills, not hits.

STATEDThe PR explicitly requires preserving promise/value identities and failure behavior for the query algorithms.

1
2
3
4
05
Success, not refresh entry, begins a turn

The backend starts a cache turn only after refresh succeeds: source cache first, graph refresh for workspace coverage, then state refresh. Selection skips graph refresh. Failure keeps the previous semantic-cache turn. That order already existed; it does not promise whole-system rollback.

STATEDThe PR says failed refresh must preserve the current successful turn, rather than clearing caches at refresh entry.

1
2
3
4
06
Erase entries before project release can settle

Release synchronously empties all six caches, then starts and awaits project release. Old cached entries are unavailable while release is pending or rejecting. Clearing does not block new queries: a query may refill a cache during the wait.

STATEDThe PR says released semantics must be unavailable while project release is pending or rejecting.

1
2
3
4
07
Move completion to the far side of project release

Backend release now waits for project release and propagates its rejection; previously it could resolve while project release was pending. The PR names this API change while also claiming failure behavior is preserved. It gives no reason reconciling those two claims.

UNEXPLAINEDAn awaited backend barrier is documented, but no rationale was found for this caller-observable timing/rejection change within a preservation-only refactor.

1
2
3
4
08
Cache locations; project nodes on every access

Position lookup still caches locations, including empty results, then rehydrates nodes each access. Its returned array is fresh even when the node object is reused. Public reference results are also projected from cached locations; cache identity is not every returned array’s identity.

STATEDThe PR requires preserving all query algorithms and value identities; the characterization commit explicitly records these existing contracts.

1
2
3
4
09
Pass the file list instead of the snapshot

The exported semantic service’s beginTurn changes from WorkspaceSnapshot to readonly WorkspaceFile[]. The backend now passes snapshot.files. The service still assigns its file list before clearing caches; a specific reason for narrowing the API was not found.

UNEXPLAINEDThe PR lists the new signature under Public surface, but gives no rationale for the narrower input contract.

1
2
3
4

Keep handles alive; clear their entries

D01
stated
Move the clearing job into core
↘

TypeScript keeps algorithms, keys, projections, and its file list. Core implements and exports the scope and handle type. Each service owns its own scope instance; the existing package dependency and process boundary stay put.

The architecture spec assigns shareable cache lifetime to core and semantic query bodies to TypeScript.

Reason & evidence ↗
D02
stated
Keep six independent stores
↘

One scope coordinates six separate Maps. Five store promises by symbol identity; the position store keeps location arrays by file and offset. Callers and references still share reference discovery.

The PR chooses six handles because the existing key and value spaces are independent.

Reason & evidence ↗

unexplained
Compose a local scope; place it under core/backend
↘

The service constructs a concrete scope in a field, rather than receiving or inheriting one. The new class lives in core/src/backend. The plan describes shared bases that backends extend.

The chosen form is disclosed. No separate reason for composition or this directory placement was found.

Reason & evidence ↗
D04
stated
Preserve entries, distinguish their projections
↘

Cache hits return the exact value, including empty results. Four direct service query methods reuse promises. Reference results and node arrays are rebuilt; backend async wrappers need not reuse the cache's promise. Miss observers still count the underlying searches.

The PR explicitly preserves all six algorithms, keys, and promise/value identities. The original rationale for reprojection is not supplied.

Reason & evidence ↗
D05
stated
Treat undefined as a present entry
↘

The generic handle uses Map.has before Map.get. Its factory can return undefined once and still get a cache hit. The six TypeScript stores already hold truthy promises or arrays; this is a broader generic contract.

The PR names undefined as a valid cached value.

Reason & evidence ↗
D06
stated
Keep rejected promises; retry synchronous throws
↘

A returned promise is stored even if it rejects. A factory throw inserts nothing. Clearing cancels neither an old promise nor its result; later settlement cannot overwrite a new entry because the scope installs no settlement callback.

Preserving existing query failure behavior and value identity is the PR's stated constraint, not a new retry policy.

Reason & evidence ↗
D07
stated
Begin the next turn after refresh succeeds
↘

Both revisions clear after source, applicable project, and workspace-state refresh succeeds—even with unchanged files. Failure skips the file-list handoff and clear. A command returning is not a clearing signal. This is a cache guarantee, not rollback of all earlier refresh effects.

The PR says failed refresh must preserve the current successful turn.

Reason & evidence ↗
D08
stated
Empty entries before starting project cleanup
↘

Clearing remains synchronous and comes first in both revisions. The unchanged graph releases projects in order and can stop on rejection; concrete TypeScript project cleanup is synchronous, even though its graph returns a promise.

Old cached semantics must be unavailable while project release is pending or rejecting, according to the PR.

Reason & evidence ↗
D09
unexplained
Extend the backend's completion and error boundary
↘

The new service and backend await graph cleanup. A held graph leaves backend release pending; rejection reaches that caller. The PR explicitly declares this barrier. How this change fits the plan's unchanged timing/failure promise is unrecorded.

The stated clear-first reason does not separately reconcile the changed completion/error contract with the broader parity requirement.

Reason & evidence ↗
D10
unexplained
Pass files across the exported service API
↘

beginTurn(snapshot) becomes beginTurn(readonly files). The backend passes snapshot.files; the service retains that same array by reference through release. Service release changes void → Promise<void>; the backend's promise signature stays the same.

The PR lists the narrowed input but gives no reason for it. The release signature belongs to the separately declared awaited barrier.

Reason & evidence ↗
D11
unexplained
Clear values while keeping handles usable
↘

The public handle exposes getOrCreate only. Both scope lifecycle methods perform the same whole-scope clear. There is no timer, turn token, closed state, cancellation, per-key invalidation, or unregister API. Handles can fill before beginTurn, after repeated release, and during pending cleanup.

The implementation and tests establish this reusable lifecycle. No separate rationale for these exact limits was found.

Reason & evidence ↗

stated
Add ten tests and retain all five existing cases
↘

Four new core cases and six new service cases pin identity, projection, failures, reset, and awaited rejection. The five old service cases and assertions are retained byte for byte. The new delayed-release case uses a rejecting graph double; it adds no delayed-success or daemon-level case.

The PR and commit subjects describe characterization and locking identity, error, and clearing contracts.
